scenario_reference.text: Dynamic Map will be capable of accepting feeds from up to 1000 sensors occurring every 60 seconds during normal operations without data loss or processing delays

analysis_records.environment: Normal operations with 1000 fixed sensors transmitting periodically
analysis_records.stimulus: 1000 sensor data feeds arriving every 60 seconds (approximately 16.7 sensor updates per second)
analysis_records.response_measure: No data loss or processing delays during continuous sensor ingestion
architectural_decisions: Data-Centric Repository with separate Traffic repository for sensor data
Publish-Subscribe pattern with buffering mechanisms for asynchronous sensor feeds
Transaction distribution across distinct repositories (Static, Traffic, Event) for parallel processing
analysis_records.reasoning: The relatively low update frequency (60-second intervals) and moderate sensor count (1000 units) results in approximately 16.7 updates per second. The Data-Centric Repository approach with buffering can handle this load through asynchronous processing. Transaction distribution across repositories reduces contention. However, without specific buffer sizes and database write throughput capacity, we cannot quantitatively verify that no data loss will occur during peak loads or bulk update scenarios.

non_risks.description: Low update frequency (60-second intervals) is well within typical database ingestion capabilities
non_risks.rationale: At 16.7 updates/second, even commodity database systems can handle this load. The publish-subscribe pattern with buffering provides additional headroom for temporary spikes.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Buffer size for sensor data ingestion queue

scenario_reference.text: System will be able to accommodate and interpret location data from 5000 GPS tracker units updated every 5 seconds, maintaining real-time accuracy for traffic visualization and route planning

analysis_records.environment: Normal operations with high-frequency GPS tracker updates
analysis_records.stimulus: 5000 GPS tracker units transmitting location data every 5 seconds (1000 updates per second)
analysis_records.response_measure: Real-time accuracy maintained for traffic visualization and route planning without processing backlog
architectural_decisions: Publish-Subscribe pattern with asynchronous buffering for GPS data streams
Separate Traffic repository to isolate high-volume GPS updates from other data
Data interpretation layer processes GPS streams for event detection and traffic analysis
analysis_records.reasoning: GPS trackers generate 1000 updates per second (5000 units / 5 seconds), which is significantly higher than fixed sensor load. The publish-subscribe pattern decouples data ingestion from processing, allowing buffering to smooth out bursts. However, sustained 1000 updates/second requires substantial database write capacity and network bandwidth. Without specific message sizes, network capacity, and database throughput metrics, this represents a significant performance risk.

risks.description: High-frequency GPS updates (1000/sec) may exceed database write capacity, causing processing backlog and delayed real-time accuracy
risks.rationale: Sustained 1000 writes per second requires high-performance database configuration. If write throughput is insufficient, buffers will fill and either data loss or increasing latency will occur. No quantitative verification of database capacity exists.

risks.description: Network bandwidth between GPS trackers and central repositories may become saturated
risks.rationale: Without knowing message sizes and available bandwidth, 1000 messages/second could exceed network capacity, especially if GPS data includes additional metadata beyond coordinates.

sensitivity_points.parameter: GPS message size (bytes per location update)
Network bandwidth capacity between GPS units and Traffic repository
Database write transaction rate (transactions per second)
Buffer capacity for GPS data ingestion queue

conflicting_attributes: Performance (real-time accuracy - positive with higher frequency)
Performance (system load and scalability - negative with higher frequency)

scenario_reference.text: Dynamic Map will be capable of processing up to 200 read queries per second from client modules (visualization, route planning, traffic control) with response times suitable for real-time decision making

analysis_records.environment: Normal operations with concurrent client query load
analysis_records.stimulus: Up to 200 read queries per second from diverse client modules
analysis_records.response_measure: Response times suitable for real-time decision making (typically sub-second for interactive applications)
architectural_decisions: Data-Centric Repository with optimized query processing for spatial data
Transaction distribution across Static, Traffic, and Event repositories reduces query contention
Layered architecture separates presentation layer from data storage, enabling query optimization
analysis_records.reasoning: 200 read queries per second is a moderate load for well-designed database systems, especially with spatial indexing. The separation of repositories (Static, Traffic, Event) allows queries to be distributed, reducing contention. However, query complexity matters significantly - simple point queries are very different from complex spatial joins. Without specific query response time requirements or query complexity profiles, we cannot definitively assess whether 'suitable for real-time decision making' will be achieved.

risks.description: Complex spatial queries (e.g., route planning with real-time traffic) may exceed response time requirements under 200 queries/sec load
risks.rationale: Route planning queries likely involve complex spatial joins across Static (road network) and Traffic (current conditions) repositories. Without query optimization strategies (caching, materialized views, spatial indexing details), complex queries may take multiple seconds, unsuitable for real-time interaction.

non_risks.description: Simple read queries (e.g., current traffic at specific location) can be served efficiently at 200 queries/sec
non_risks.rationale: Point queries with spatial indexing typically execute in milliseconds. Repository separation reduces lock contention, allowing parallel query execution.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Query complexity distribution (simple vs. complex spatial queries)
Spatial indexing strategy and database configuration
Acceptable response time threshold for 'real-time decision making'

tradeoff_points.parameter: Repository normalization (separate Static, Traffic, Event repositories)
conflicting_attributes: Performance (reduced contention through transaction distribution - positive)
Performance (complex queries requiring joins across repositories - negative)

scenario_reference.text: New sensor types and sensor processing software will be integrated into the system within 6 days, including data collection modules, repository schema updates, and client interface modifications

analysis_records.environment: System evolution requiring integration of new sensor technology
analysis_records.stimulus: Request to add new sensor type with associated processing logic
analysis_records.response_measure: Complete integration (data collection, storage, processing, presentation) within 6 days
architectural_decisions: Layered architecture isolates sensor-specific concerns to data collection layer
Data-Centric Repository with extensible schema supports new data types
Ontology-based definitions enable semantic integration of new sensor data
Publish-Subscribe pattern allows new processing modules to subscribe to sensor feeds without modifying producers
analysis_records.reasoning: The layered architecture and publish-subscribe pattern provide strong modifiability support. New sensors can be added by creating data collection modules that publish to existing repositories, and new processing modules can subscribe to these feeds. However, 6 days is an aggressive timeline that requires well-defined interfaces, comprehensive documentation, and minimal coupling between components. Repository schema updates could require data migration and client interface modifications introduce cross-layer dependencies.

risks.description: Repository schema updates for new sensor data types may require data migration and extensive testing, potentially exceeding 6-day timeline
risks.rationale: Adding new columns or tables to spatial repositories with existing data requires careful migration planning. If schema changes affect existing queries or require index rebuilding, downtime and testing could extend beyond 6 days.

risks.description: Client interface modifications introduce cross-layer dependencies that may cascade changes beyond data collection layer
risks.rationale: If new sensor data requires presentation layer changes (new visualization types, user controls), the layered architecture's modifiability benefits are reduced. Changes propagate across multiple layers, increasing integration time.

non_risks.description: Adding new sensor data collection modules without schema changes can be accomplished quickly through publish-subscribe pattern
non_risks.rationale: If new sensor data fits existing repository schema (e.g., another GPS tracker type), only data collection module development is needed. Publish-subscribe decoupling allows independent deployment.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Degree of schema change required for new sensor type
Ontology extensibility for new sensor semantics

tradeoff_points.parameter: Repository schema flexibility (generic vs. sensor-specific schemas)
conflicting_attributes: Modifiability (adding new sensor types without schema changes - positive with generic schema)
Performance (query optimization for specific sensor types - negative with overly generic schema)

scenario_reference.text: Sensor failures will be detected in a configurable period ranging from 3 to 20 minutes through monitoring of expected periodic updates, enabling automated alerts and failover mechanisms

analysis_records.environment: Normal operations with potential sensor hardware failures
analysis_records.stimulus: Sensor stops transmitting periodic updates due to hardware failure or network disconnection
analysis_records.response_measure: Failure detected within configurable 3-20 minute window, triggering automated alerts
architectural_decisions: Publish-Subscribe pattern with expected update intervals enables timeout-based failure detection
Decoupled sensor feeds allow system to continue operating despite individual sensor failures
Event repository can log failure events for monitoring and alerting
analysis_records.reasoning: The publish-subscribe architecture naturally supports failure detection through monitoring of expected periodic updates. Since sensors publish at known intervals (60 seconds for fixed sensors, 5 seconds for GPS), absence of updates within expected timeframes indicates failure. The 3-20 minute configurable window provides flexibility for different sensor types and network conditions. Decoupled architecture ensures individual sensor failures don't cascade to system-wide failures.

non_risks.description: Publish-subscribe pattern with known update intervals provides robust foundation for timeout-based failure detection
non_risks.rationale: Expected update intervals (60s for fixed sensors, 5s for GPS) are well-defined. Monitoring modules can easily detect missing updates within 3-20 minute window. Decoupled architecture prevents failure propagation.

non_risks.description: Configurable detection window (3-20 minutes) accommodates different sensor types and network reliability levels
non_risks.rationale: Flexibility in detection timing reduces false positives from temporary network issues while ensuring timely detection of genuine failures. Different sensor types can have different thresholds.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Failure detection window configuration (3-20 minute range)
sensitivity_points.correlated_attribute: Reliability (false positive rate vs. detection latency)

conflicting_attributes: Reliability (rapid failure detection - positive with shorter window)
Reliability (false positive reduction - positive with longer window)

scenario_reference.text: Updating of data defining the road network (static repository modifications) can cause a loss of at most 10 values of a single monitoring parameter during the transition period, ensuring data integrity

analysis_records.environment: Road network updates requiring static repository schema or data modifications
analysis_records.stimulus: Administrative update to road network definition (new roads, changed topology, updated attributes)
analysis_records.response_measure: Maximum 10 values of a single monitoring parameter lost during update transition
architectural_decisions: Separation of Static repository (road network) from Traffic repository (dynamic sensor data)
Transaction isolation mechanisms to manage concurrent reads during schema updates
Buffering of sensor data during repository updates to minimize data loss
analysis_records.reasoning: The separation of Static and Traffic repositories allows road network updates to occur with limited impact on ongoing sensor data collection. However, if road network topology changes (e.g., road segments renumbered), sensor data referencing old topology may become orphaned. The 10-value loss limit suggests a brief transition period where data mapping is ambiguous. Without specific transaction management and data migration strategies, this requirement is at risk.

risks.description: Road network topology changes may orphan more than 10 sensor values if referential integrity mechanisms are insufficient
risks.rationale: If road segments are renumbered or removed, sensor data referencing those segments may be lost or misattributed. Without documented data migration procedures or referential integrity constraints, the 10-value limit may be exceeded during complex topology changes.

risks.description: Concurrent sensor updates during Static repository modifications may cause data inconsistency beyond 10-value threshold
risks.rationale: If 1000 sensors update every 60 seconds and 5000 GPS units update every 5 seconds, during a multi-second repository update window, hundreds of sensor values could reference inconsistent road network state. Transaction isolation strategy is critical but not specified.

non_risks.description: Repository separation limits scope of data loss to parameters directly dependent on modified road network elements
non_risks.rationale: Traffic and Event repositories remain operational during Static repository updates. Only sensor data explicitly referencing modified road segments is at risk, limiting potential data loss.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Transaction isolation level during Static repository updates
Duration of road network update transaction window
sensitivity_points.correlated_attribute: Reliability (number of sensor values at risk)

sensitivity_points.parameter: Referential integrity enforcement between Static and Traffic repositories

tradeoff_points.parameter: Repository normalization (separate Static and Traffic repositories)
conflicting_attributes: Reliability (referential integrity during concurrent updates - negative)

scenario_reference.text: New event types and corresponding customizable detection routines can be introduced in 1 day using ontology-based definitions without requiring changes to core repository structure

analysis_records.environment: System evolution requiring new event detection capabilities
analysis_records.stimulus: Request to add new event type (e.g., new traffic incident category) with custom detection logic
analysis_records.response_measure: Complete integration of new event type and detection routine within 1 day
architectural_decisions: Ontology-based event definitions enable semantic extensibility without schema changes
Event repository designed with flexible schema to accommodate new event types
Data interpretation layer supports pluggable detection routines that subscribe to sensor data streams
Publish-subscribe pattern allows new detection modules to be added without modifying data sources
analysis_records.reasoning: The 1-day timeline is achievable if the ontology-based approach is well-implemented and detection routines can be added as independent modules. The publish-subscribe pattern supports this by allowing new subscribers (detection routines) to consume existing sensor data streams. However, this assumes detection logic can be implemented, tested, and deployed rapidly, and that ontology extensions don't require complex semantic reasoning or validation.

non_risks.description: Ontology-based event definitions with flexible Event repository schema enable rapid addition of new event types
non_risks.rationale: If Event repository uses extensible schema (e.g., key-value attributes, JSON documents), new event types can be added without schema migration. Ontology provides semantic definitions without code changes.

non_risks.description: Publish-subscribe pattern allows new detection routines to be deployed as independent subscribers without modifying sensor data sources
non_risks.rationale: Detection modules can subscribe to existing Traffic and Event data streams, process data according to new logic, and publish detected events. Decoupled architecture enables rapid deployment.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Ontology extension complexity (simple attribute addition vs. complex semantic relationships)
Detection routine complexity (simple threshold-based vs. complex pattern recognition)

scenario_reference.text: New map features can be introduced and made discoverable with built-in functionality, allowing client modules to dynamically detect and utilize new capabilities without manual reconfiguration

analysis_records.environment: System evolution with new visualization or analysis features
analysis_records.stimulus: Introduction of new map feature (e.g., new data layer, visualization mode, or analysis capability)
analysis_records.response_measure: Client modules automatically discover and utilize new features without manual reconfiguration
architectural_decisions: Layered architecture with well-defined interfaces between presentation and data layers
Service discovery or capability advertisement mechanism for dynamic feature detection
Ontology-based feature definitions enable semantic discovery of new capabilities
analysis_records.reasoning: Dynamic feature discovery requires a metadata or service registry mechanism where new features can advertise their capabilities and client modules can query available features. This is architecturally feasible but requires additional infrastructure beyond the basic Data-Centric Repository and Layered patterns. Without explicit service discovery mechanisms documented in the architectural approaches, this scenario represents a potential gap.

risks.description: No explicit service discovery or capability advertisement mechanism documented in architectural approaches
risks.rationale: While ontology-based definitions support semantic extensibility, dynamic feature discovery requires runtime metadata exchange between presentation layer and data/interpretation layers. Without documented service registry or capability query interfaces, client modules cannot automatically discover new features.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Service discovery mechanism implementation (registry-based, query-based, or advertisement-based)
Feature metadata richness (simple availability flags vs. detailed capability descriptions)
sensitivity_points.correlated_attribute: Usability (client ability to utilize discovered features effectively)

conflicting_attributes: Modifiability (automatic client adaptation to new features - positive)
Performance (runtime overhead of capability queries and metadata exchange - negative)

scenario_reference.text: A Dynamic Map component can be ported to another platform within 20 days by isolating platform-specific dependencies to individual architectural layers

analysis_records.environment: System deployment on new hardware or software platform
analysis_records.stimulus: Request to port a system component (e.g., data collection module, repository, or client interface) to different platform
analysis_records.response_measure: Complete porting including adaptation, testing, and deployment within 20 days
architectural_decisions: Layered architecture isolates platform-specific concerns to individual layers
Well-defined interfaces between layers enable independent platform adaptation
Data-Centric Repository abstracts storage mechanisms from application logic
analysis_records.reasoning: The layered architecture provides good portability support by isolating platform dependencies. For example, porting a client interface to a new GUI framework affects only the presentation layer, while porting a repository to a new database platform affects only the data storage layer. The 20-day timeline is reasonable for single-component porting with well-defined interfaces. However, portability depends heavily on interface stability and the degree of platform-specific code in each layer.

risks.description: Cross-layer dependencies or platform-specific optimizations may require changes beyond the target component layer
risks.rationale: If components use platform-specific features for performance optimization (e.g., database-specific spatial queries, OS-specific threading), porting may require changes across multiple layers. Without documented interface contracts and platform abstraction layers, 20-day timeline is at risk.

non_risks.description: Layered architecture with clear separation of concerns supports component-level portability
non_risks.rationale: If platform-specific code is truly isolated to individual layers and interfaces are platform-agnostic, porting a single component requires only adaptation of that layer. Well-defined interfaces enable independent testing and deployment.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Degree of platform-specific optimization in component implementation
Interface abstraction level between layers (platform-agnostic vs. platform-exposed)

conflicting_attributes: Performance (leveraging platform-specific features for optimization - positive)
Portability (ease of porting to different platforms - negative)

evaluation_inputs.system_description: The EOSDIS Core System (ECS) is a large-scale, distributed data management system for NASA's Earth Observing System (EOS). Its primary purpose is to ingest, process, archive, and distribute massive amounts of earth science data collected from satellites (such as Terra, Aqua, and Landsat) and other sensors. The system is designed to operate 24/7, handling hundreds of gigabytes of raw data daily, processing it into higher-level data products using science algorithms, and making this information searchable and available to the worldwide scientific community. It features a distributed architecture spanning four major data centers in the U.S., integrating custom code with numerous COTS products.

phase_1_discovery.initial_documentation_status: The system was already fielded and supported by volumes of documentation, including architecture documents provided by the client. The evaluation team reviewed these materials beforehand to understand the system's broad details and concept of operations.

scenario_reference.text: During peak ingest, the system processes incoming data streams without backlog, maintaining data availability for algorithms.

analysis_records.stimulus: High-volume data stream arrival
analysis_records.response_measure: Zero processing backlog; data remains available for algorithms
architectural_decisions: Distributed Object / Client-Server architecture across four data centers
Load Balancing across ~20 Unix servers per site
Pipe-and-Filter for data processing pipelines
analysis_records.reasoning: The distributed architecture and load balancing allow horizontal scaling to handle peak ingest by spreading the load. The pipe-and-filter pattern enables parallel processing stages. However, the performance depends on the ingest rate vs. aggregate processing capacity. Without specific data rates and server capacities, a bottleneck risk exists if the peak rate exceeds planned capacity.

risks.description: Peak ingest data rate may exceed the aggregate processing capacity of the distributed servers, causing backlog.
risks.rationale: Without quantitative data on peak ingest rate and per-server processing throughput, the system's ability to meet the 'no backlog' goal cannot be verified. The architecture scales horizontally, but there may be a maximum ingest rate the current deployment can handle.

risks.description: Network bandwidth between data centers could become a bottleneck for data replication during peak ingest, affecting availability for algorithms at other sites.
risks.rationale: Data replication is critical for availability. If ingest volume saturates inter-data-center links, replication latency increases, potentially making data 'unavailable' at remote sites for algorithms that require the latest data.

non_risks.description: Single server failure during peak ingest will not cause system-wide backlog due to load balancing and redundancy.
non_risks.rationale: The load balancing approach and distribution across multiple servers ensure that if one server fails, its load can be redistributed to others, maintaining overall processing throughput.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Number of active processing servers per data center

scenario_reference.text: A science algorithm run on a standard dataset completes within its allocated processing slot to meet distribution schedules.

analysis_records.stimulus: Initiation of a science algorithm run on a standard dataset
analysis_records.response_measure: Algorithm completion within its allocated time slot
architectural_decisions: Pipe-and-Filter for data processing
Load Balancing across servers
Layered Architecture isolating algorithm execution
analysis_records.reasoning: The pipe-and-filter pattern allows modular, potentially parallel execution of algorithm stages. Load balancing ensures computational resources are allocated efficiently. The layered architecture helps manage dependencies. The key risk is algorithm complexity or data size causing overruns, especially if multiple algorithms run concurrently competing for resources.

risks.description: Unbounded algorithm execution time due to variable dataset sizes or computational complexity may cause missed schedules.
risks.rationale: Without a defined 'standard dataset size' and known algorithm performance profiles, it is unclear if the allocated slots are sufficient. Concurrent executions could also lead to resource contention.

non_risks.description: The layered architecture promotes maintainability, allowing performance-optimized replacements for slow algorithm components without system-wide changes.
non_risks.rationale: Separation of concerns means a poorly performing algorithm module can be refactored or replaced independently, mitigating long-term performance risk.

scenario_reference.text: Data replicated across four data centers remains consistent and uncorrupted after a site network partition is resolved.

analysis_records.environment: System experiencing a network partition between one or more data centers
analysis_records.stimulus: Network partition occurs and is later resolved
analysis_records.response_measure: Data consistency and integrity are maintained across all data centers post-recovery
architectural_decisions: Data Replication and Archiving across four data centers
Distributed Object / Client-Server architecture
analysis_records.reasoning: Data replication provides redundancy. However, maintaining consistency during a partition requires a reconciliation strategy (e.g., conflict resolution). The client-server model may rely on synchronous or asynchronous replication. Without details on the replication protocol, there is a risk of divergence or data loss.

risks.description: Network partitions can lead to split-brain scenarios where conflicting updates are made at different sites, causing data inconsistency upon reconnection.
risks.rationale: The architectural description does not specify the consistency model (e.g., strong vs. eventual) or conflict resolution mechanisms. This is a classic risk in distributed, replicated systems.

non_risks.description: The multi-site replication inherently provides durability against a single site failure, protecting data from physical loss.
non_risks.rationale: Even with temporary inconsistency, the data is not lost; it exists in at least one other site. The architecture provides a strong foundation for recovery.

scenario_reference.text: If a Unix server fails at a data center, its workload is redistributed without loss of ingested data or interruption to active algorithm runs.

analysis_records.stimulus: A Unix server fails
analysis_records.response_measure: Workload redistributed; no data loss or interruption to active algorithms
architectural_decisions: Load Balancing (implied)
Data Replication and Archiving
analysis_records.reasoning: Load balancing allows traffic to be redirected to healthy servers. For no data loss, ingested data must be persisted before the failure (e.g., via replication or durable queues). Active algorithm runs may be checkpointed or restarted on another server. The architecture supports this, but implementation details (e.g., stateless vs. stateful components) are critical.

risks.description: Loss of in-memory, unpersisted data from the failed server if ingest buffers or algorithm state are not checkpointed.
risks.rationale: If servers hold transient data during processing and fail before persisting to shared storage, that data may be lost unless a replication/checkpointing mechanism is in place.

non_risks.description: The distributed nature and multiple servers per site make workload redistribution technically feasible and a standard practice.
non_risks.rationale: The architecture explicitly includes about 20 servers per site, providing a pool for failover. Load balancers can detect failure and redirect requests.

scenario_reference.text: The archive and processing infrastructure can accommodate a 20% year-over-year increase in data volume without degrading performance for standard user queries.

analysis_records.environment: Steady state with annual 20% data volume growth
analysis_records.stimulus: Data volume increases by 20% per year
analysis_records.response_measure: No degradation in performance for standard user queries
architectural_decisions: Data Replication and Archiving
Distributed Object / Client-Server
Layered Architecture
analysis_records.reasoning: The distributed architecture is designed for horizontal scaling—adding more servers or storage nodes can handle increased volume. However, scaling must be planned and may require additional hardware investment. The layered architecture helps isolate query performance from archive growth. Risks include unforeseen bottlenecks in network or metadata management.

risks.description: Centralized components (e.g., name servers, metadata catalogs) may become bottlenecks as data volume grows, impacting query performance.
risks.rationale: While data storage scales, the services that index and locate data (common in client-server architectures) might not scale linearly and could become a performance limiter.

non_risks.description: The use of distributed data centers and archiving provides a clear path for capacity expansion by adding storage nodes or entire sites.
non_risks.rationale: The architectural style is inherently scalable by adding more nodes to the network, a proven approach for handling data growth.

scenario_reference.text: The system supports a 50% increase in concurrently executing external science algorithms without modification to core orchestration services.

analysis_records.stimulus: Number of concurrent external algorithm executions increases by 50%
analysis_records.response_measure: Core orchestration services require no modification to support the increase
architectural_decisions: Layered Architecture
Pipe-and-Filter
Load Balancing
analysis_records.reasoning: Layered architecture decouples orchestration services from algorithm execution. Pipe-and-filter allows parallel pipelines. Load balancing distributes the increased load. The core risk is that orchestration services (e.g., job schedulers, resource managers) may have internal limits (e.g., number of concurrent jobs tracked) that are exceeded.

risks.description: Orchestration service capacity limits (e.g., max concurrent jobs, thread pools, database connections) may be reached before the 50% increase, requiring reconfiguration or code changes.
risks.rationale: Even with a layered design, the orchestration component itself has finite resources. Its scalability limits are not specified in the architectural approaches.

non_risks.description: The pipe-and-filter pattern allows new algorithm instances to be added as independent processes/containers, scaling horizontally.
non_risks.rationale: The pattern supports adding more filter instances to handle increased concurrency, aligning with the scalability goal.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Orchestration service's maximum concurrent job limit
Resource pool size (CPU, memory) available for algorithms

analysis_records.response_measure: Report generated and delivered within 2 hours
architectural_decisions: Layered Architecture

analysis_records.reasoning: Layered architecture likely separates reporting functions, allowing efficient querying of archived results. Data replication ensures result data is available. The 2-hour deadline depends on report complexity, data retrieval speed, and system load. A risk is if generating the report requires computationally expensive reprocessing.

risks.description: Report generation may require aggregating large volumes of data from distributed archives, exceeding the 2-hour window if network or query performance is poor.
risks.rationale: Without knowing the size of typical result datasets and the performance of the reporting query layer, the time constraint may be at risk.

non_risks.description: The layered architecture isolates reporting tools, allowing them to be optimized for performance without affecting core processing pipelines.
non_risks.rationale: Separation of concerns means the reporting layer can be independently scaled or tuned to meet its specific performance requirements.

scenario_reference.text: Common failures in data ingest or COTS product communication are detected and remediated automatically, alerting operators only for escalation.

analysis_records.stimulus: A common failure (e.g., ingest stream interruption, COTS heartbeat loss) occurs

architectural_decisions: Layered Architecture
Integration with numerous COTS products

Integration with many COTS products increases complexity—each may have unique failure signatures and recovery procedures.

risks.description: COTS product failures may be opaque or lack APIs for automated remediation, forcing manual operator intervention and violating the 'automatic' goal.
risks.rationale: COTS products are black-box components; their internal failures may not be detectable or recoverable via external automation, increasing operability burden.

non_risks.description: The layered structure provides clear points for inserting health checks and monitoring agents for custom components.
non_risks.rationale: Standard interfaces between layers are natural places to implement fault detection and recovery logic for the custom parts of the system.

However, if COTS products are tightly coupled or directly define data formats, an upgrade may force format changes. The 'one development cycle' timeline depends on the complexity of integration testing.

risks.rationale: Even with a layered design, if the COTS product is the originator of a critical data format, a version change may force a format change, violating the scenario goal.

non_risks.description: The layered architecture principle of separation allows the COTS product to be wrapped, limiting the blast radius of changes to its specific layer.
non_risks.rationale: Good practice of using abstraction layers (e.g., adapters) minimizes the impact of COTS changes on the rest of the system.

tradeoff_points.parameter: Adapter layer generality (thick vs. thin wrapper)

scenarios.scenario_text: An operator requests a report for the execution results of a specific scientific algorithm run. The system must generate and deliver the complete report within 2 hours of the request during normal operations.
During peak data collection periods with 500+ concurrent sensors transmitting, the ECS must maintain response times under 3 seconds for operator queries and commands without degradation.
The system must scale to accommodate a 300% increase in sensor count (from current baseline to projected growth) over 3 years without requiring architectural redesign.
When a critical sensor data processing component fails, the system must detect the failure within 30 seconds and automatically failover to redundant components with zero data loss.
The ECS must achieve 99.5% uptime annually, with no single planned maintenance window exceeding 4 hours and no more than 6 planned maintenance events per year.
A developer must be able to deploy a software update to the data processing pipeline with zero downtime using rolling deployment strategies, completing the full deployment within 1 hour.

When integrating a new third-party sensor type with different data formats, a developer must be able to add the necessary data transformation components within 2 weeks without modifying core system architecture.
All sensor data ingested into the system must maintain complete integrity with cryptographic verification, detecting any corruption or tampering with 100% accuracy within 1 minute of data receipt.
During a network bandwidth reduction event (50% capacity loss), the system must prioritize critical telemetry data and maintain delivery of high-priority data streams with less than 5% packet loss.
An operator must be able to configure new data collection parameters and deploy them to 100+ sensors within 15 minutes using the ECS management interface without requiring developer assistance.

The system must support interoperability with external scientific analysis tools by exposing standardized APIs (REST/GraphQL) that allow third-party applications to query historical sensor data with response times under 2 seconds for 90% of queries.

When daily data volume grows from current 5TB to projected 20TB within 2 years, the system must handle the increased throughput without requiring hardware infrastructure changes beyond linear scaling of storage.
A new operations team member must be able to perform routine monitoring tasks (checking sensor health, viewing dashboards, acknowledging alerts) within 1 day of training using intuitive interfaces.
The system must automatically archive sensor data older than 90 days to cold storage while maintaining query access with response times under 10 seconds for archived data retrieval.
When a software defect is identified in the data validation module, a developer must be able to isolate, test, and deploy a fix within 48 hours without impacting other system components.

evaluation_inputs.system_description: A component-based software architecture designed to facilitate game portability across different commercial and bespoke game engines. The core concept employs a 'game space' component that services game logic (plot/story) to multiple game engines (views) without requiring modification to the game itself. It utilizes a variant of the Model-View-Controller pattern where the game space acts as the Model and the game engines act as Views, connected via Adapters.

analysis_records.stimulus: New COTS game engine API specification becomes available

Adapters co-located with game space to minimize integration complexity
Component-based architecture enables independent adapter development
analysis_records.reasoning: The adapter pattern is the primary mechanism enabling this scenario. Since game logic is isolated in the game space, supporting a new engine requires only developing a new adapter that translates between the game space's canonical representation and the new engine's proprietary format. The 2-week timeline depends on adapter complexity, API documentation quality, and the degree of similarity to previously supported engines.

risks.description: Incomplete or ambiguous COTS engine API specification may delay adapter development beyond 2 weeks
risks.rationale: Adapter development requires complete understanding of engine's state representation, event model, and rendering pipeline. Gaps in API documentation require reverse engineering or vendor consultation.

risks.description: COTS engine may have architectural assumptions incompatible with game space model
risks.rationale: Some engines may assume tight coupling between game logic and rendering, or may not support the distributed architecture pattern, requiring significant adapter workarounds.

non_risks.description: Game space logic remains stable during adapter development
non_risks.rationale: The adapter pattern ensures game logic isolation, so no modifications to core game space are required regardless of engine complexity.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Semantic gap between game space representation and engine representation
Adapter developer familiarity with engine API

conflicting_attributes: Portability (higher abstraction simplifies supporting diverse engines)

scenario_reference.text: Migrate existing game to bespoke engine without modifying game logic code

analysis_records.environment: Production system migration from one engine platform to another
analysis_records.stimulus: Decision to migrate game from current engine to bespoke engine
analysis_records.response_measure: Migration completed with zero changes to game logic code
architectural_decisions: MVC variant separates game logic (Model) from rendering (View)
Game space encapsulates all game logic in engine-agnostic format
Adapter layer provides complete isolation between game space and engine
analysis_records.reasoning: The MVC variant architecture ensures game logic is completely independent of the rendering platform. Migration requires only developing a new adapter for the bespoke engine while the game space remains unchanged. This validates the core portability goal of the architecture.

risks.description: Bespoke engine may lack features assumed by game logic, requiring game space modifications
risks.rationale: If game logic implicitly depends on engine capabilities (e.g., specific physics simulation, audio features), the adapter alone cannot bridge the gap.

non_risks.description: Adapter pattern guarantees game logic isolation from engine specifics
non_risks.rationale: The architectural approach explicitly separates game state/behavior from engine representation, making zero-modification migration architecturally feasible.

non_risks.description: Existing adapters remain functional during migration
non_risks.rationale: Component-based architecture allows parallel operation of multiple adapters, enabling gradual migration or multi-engine support.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Degree of feature parity between old and new engines

analysis_records.response_measure: New behavior active without recompilation or restart
architectural_decisions: Scripting engine integration supports both internal and external behavior engines
Runtime script loading capability enabled despite performance penalty
Game space architecture supports dynamic behavior injection
analysis_records.reasoning: The scripting engine integration provides runtime modifiability at the cost of 10x performance penalty. This architectural decision prioritizes flexibility over execution efficiency, enabling live game updates and rapid iteration during development.

risks.description: 10x performance penalty may violate performance scenarios if scripted behaviors are on critical path
risks.rationale: If scripted behaviors execute during frame rendering or state updates, the performance degradation could prevent achieving 20 FPS target or <200ms response time.

risks.description: Runtime script errors could crash game space without restart capability
risks.rationale: Dynamic script loading introduces runtime stability risks if scripts are not properly validated or sandboxed.

non_risks.description: Scripting engine isolation prevents script errors from corrupting core game state
non_risks.rationale: If scripting engine is properly sandboxed, script failures can be contained without affecting pre-compiled game logic.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Proportion of game logic implemented in scripts vs. pre-compiled code
Script validation and error handling robustness

tradeoff_points.parameter: Use of scripting engine for behavior implementation
conflicting_attributes: Modifiability (scripting enables runtime changes without recompilation)

analysis_records.environment: Maintenance phase with game engine vendor API update
analysis_records.stimulus: Game engine vendor releases API update with breaking changes
analysis_records.response_measure: Adapter updated and tested within 3 days
architectural_decisions: Adapter pattern localizes engine-specific code to adapter component
Component-based architecture enables independent adapter evolution
Adapters co-located with game space for simplified deployment
analysis_records.reasoning: The adapter pattern localizes the impact of engine API changes to a single component. The 3-day timeline assumes the adapter is well-structured and the API changes are documented. Co-location with game space simplifies testing and deployment.

risks.description: Breaking API changes may require fundamental adapter redesign exceeding 3-day timeline
risks.rationale: If engine vendor changes core architectural assumptions (e.g., synchronous to asynchronous API), adapter may require substantial rework.

risks.description: Adapter update may introduce regressions affecting game functionality
risks.rationale: Without comprehensive integration tests, adapter changes risk breaking existing game behaviors that depend on subtle engine interactions.

non_risks.description: Game space and other adapters remain unaffected by engine API changes
non_risks.rationale: Adapter pattern ensures changes are localized to the affected adapter component only.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Scope and documentation quality of engine API changes
Adapter code modularity and test coverage

scenario_reference.text: Modify game logic without requiring changes to existing game engine adapters

analysis_records.environment: Development phase with game logic enhancements
analysis_records.stimulus: Game designer modifies game rules or adds new game mechanics
analysis_records.response_measure: Game logic changes deployed without adapter modifications
architectural_decisions: MVC variant separates game logic from presentation concerns
Game space defines stable interface contract with adapters
Adapter translates between stable game space representation and engine format
analysis_records.reasoning: The MVC separation ensures game logic changes do not propagate to adapters as long as the game space interface contract remains stable. This enables independent evolution of game content and rendering platforms.

risks.description: New game mechanics may introduce state elements not representable in current adapter interface
risks.rationale: If new game logic requires new types of state or events not anticipated in the adapter interface design, adapters must be updated to support them.

non_risks.description: Game logic changes within existing state model do not affect adapters
non_risks.rationale: As long as changes involve only game rules and behavior within the existing state representation, adapters remain valid.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Stability and extensibility of game space interface contract

conflicting_attributes: Modifiability (higher abstraction accommodates more game logic changes without adapter impact)
Performance (higher abstraction may require more complex adapter translations)

scenario_reference.text: Execute scripted behavior with response time <200ms despite 10x performance penalty compared to pre-compiled code

analysis_records.environment: Runtime execution with scripted behavior invocation
analysis_records.stimulus: Game event triggers scripted behavior execution
analysis_records.response_measure: Scripted behavior completes within 200ms
architectural_decisions: Scripting engine integration accepts 10x performance penalty for modifiability
Behavior execution architecture supports both scripted and pre-compiled paths
Performance budget allocated for scripted behavior execution
analysis_records.reasoning: This scenario quantifies the performance cost of runtime modifiability. The 200ms target with 10x penalty implies pre-compiled equivalent would execute in 20ms. This is achievable for most game behaviors but constrains the complexity of scriptable logic.

risks.description: Complex scripted behaviors may exceed 200ms budget given 10x penalty
risks.rationale: If scripted behavior requires >20ms in pre-compiled form (e.g., complex AI, pathfinding), the 10x penalty makes 200ms target unachievable.

risks.description: Cascading scripted behavior invocations may accumulate latency beyond acceptable limits
risks.rationale: If one scripted behavior triggers others, cumulative latency could violate user experience requirements even if individual behaviors meet 200ms target.

non_risks.description: Simple event handlers and state updates remain well within 200ms budget
non_risks.rationale: Most game behaviors involve simple state changes or event dispatching that execute in <5ms pre-compiled, leaving comfortable margin even with 10x penalty.

conflicting_attributes: Modifiability (broader scripting scope enables more runtime flexibility)
Performance (broader scripting scope increases likelihood of performance violations)

scenario_reference.text: Maintain 20 FPS display rate with network latency between game space and game engine <50ms

analysis_records.environment: Normal operations with distributed game space and engine
analysis_records.stimulus: Continuous game state updates and rendering cycles
analysis_records.response_measure: Sustained 20 FPS (50ms frame time) with network latency <50ms
architectural_decisions: Distributed architecture separates game space and engine across network
Adapters co-located with game space to minimize translation overhead
Network communication optimized for state synchronization
analysis_records.reasoning: The 20 FPS target requires 50ms total frame time. With network latency consuming up to 50ms, this leaves minimal budget for game logic execution, adapter translation, and rendering. The architecture must carefully manage state synchronization to avoid frame drops.

risks.description: Network latency approaching 50ms leaves insufficient time for game logic and rendering within 50ms frame budget
risks.rationale: If network latency is 50ms, game logic execution, adapter translation, and engine rendering must complete in near-zero time, which is infeasible for non-trivial games.

risks.description: Network latency variability (jitter) may cause intermittent frame drops even when average latency is acceptable
risks.rationale: Network jitter can cause individual frames to exceed 50ms total time even if average latency is well below 50ms.

risks.description: State synchronization overhead may compound with network latency to violate frame budget
risks.rationale: Adapter must serialize game state, transmit over network, and deserialize on engine side. This overhead adds to network latency and may exceed 50ms total.

non_risks.description: Distributed architecture offloads game logic from engine machine, reducing rendering bottlenecks
non_risks.rationale: By separating game logic processing, the engine machine can dedicate resources to rendering, improving frame rate stability.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Game state size and update frequency

conflicting_attributes: Modifiability (distributed architecture enables independent scaling and deployment)
Performance (distributed architecture introduces network latency that constrains frame rate)
Portability (fine-grained updates provide more flexibility for diverse engine representations)

scenario_reference.text: Support 100 concurrent game state updates per second across network boundary

analysis_records.environment: High-activity gameplay with frequent state changes
analysis_records.stimulus: Game logic generates 100 state updates per second
analysis_records.response_measure: All updates transmitted and processed within frame deadlines
architectural_decisions: Distributed architecture with network-based state synchronization
Adapter manages batching and prioritization of state updates
Network protocol optimized for high-frequency small messages
analysis_records.reasoning: 100 updates/second means one update every 10ms. With 20 FPS target (50ms frames), this allows 5 updates per frame. The adapter must efficiently batch and transmit updates to avoid overwhelming the network or engine.

risks.description: 100 updates/second may saturate network bandwidth if updates are not efficiently encoded
risks.rationale: Without compression or delta encoding, high update frequency can consume excessive bandwidth, increasing latency and jitter.

risks.description: Update processing overhead on engine side may prevent achieving 20 FPS if updates are not batched
risks.rationale: Processing 5 individual updates per frame adds overhead. Batching updates reduces per-update processing cost but increases complexity.

non_risks.description: 100 updates/second is manageable with efficient batching and delta encoding
non_risks.rationale: Modern network protocols and serialization techniques can handle this update rate with minimal overhead if properly optimized.

conflicting_attributes: Performance (larger batches increase latency between state change and rendering)

scenario_reference.text: Adapter translation overhead <10ms per frame for state synchronization

analysis_records.stimulus: Adapter translates game state to engine format each frame
analysis_records.response_measure: Translation completes within 10ms
architectural_decisions: Adapters co-located with game space to minimize communication overhead
Adapter uses efficient serialization and translation algorithms
Adapter caches translated state to minimize redundant work
analysis_records.reasoning: With 50ms frame budget and up to 50ms network latency, the 10ms adapter overhead target is critical. This leaves 40ms for network transmission and engine rendering, which is tight but feasible with optimization.

risks.description: Complex game state representations may require >10ms translation time
risks.rationale: If game state includes complex data structures (e.g., large scene graphs, detailed physics state), translation to engine format may exceed 10ms budget.

risks.description: Adapter translation time may scale poorly with game state complexity
risks.rationale: As games grow in complexity, state size increases, potentially causing translation time to exceed 10ms in later development stages.

non_risks.description: Co-location of adapter with game space eliminates inter-process communication overhead
non_risks.rationale: Running adapter in same process as game space avoids serialization and IPC costs, keeping translation overhead minimal.

non_risks.description: Delta encoding and caching can reduce translation overhead for unchanged state
non_risks.rationale: Most game state remains stable between frames. Translating only changed elements significantly reduces per-frame overhead.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Semantic gap between game space and engine representations

conflicting_attributes: Portability (higher abstraction supports more diverse engines)
Performance (higher abstraction increases translation complexity and overhead)

evaluation_inputs.system_description: A reference architecture designed to standardize interfaces between software components for various ground-based command and control systems. phase_1_discovery.initial_documentation_status: The reference architecture was partially documented. The team had developed high-level Interface Design Language (IDL) and completed approximately one-fourth of the IDL for the 12 identified sub-domains. The specification was not complete.

scenario_reference.text: A system integrator incorporates a new vendor component into the system.

analysis_records.stimulus: Need to integrate a new vendor component
analysis_records.response_measure: Integration within 48 hours using standard IDL
architectural_decisions: Mandated use of CORBA with IDL
Standardized communication protocols
analysis_records.reasoning: CORBA's IDL provides a language-neutral interface definition, theoretically enabling 'plug-and-play' integration. The 48-hour goal assumes the new component's interface is fully compliant with the existing IDL and the ORB implementations are compatible.

risks.description: Vendor's CORBA ORB implementation may have proprietary extensions or version incompatibilities that break interoperability.
risks.rationale: Even with standard IDL, different ORB vendors may have subtle differences in protocol support, QoS features, or marshaling, causing integration delays.

risks.description: The new component's semantic behavior may not match system expectations despite syntactic IDL compatibility.
risks.rationale: IDL defines syntax but not semantics (e.g., valid parameter ranges, stateful behavior). Misalignment can cause functional errors post-integration.

non_risks.description: Syntactic interface mismatch is mitigated by the mandated CORBA IDL standard.
non_risks.rationale: The IDL serves as a contract. If both parties adhere strictly, the basic communication plumbing is standardized.

scenario_reference.text: Operator issues a time-critical command to a remote sensor during a mission.

analysis_records.stimulus: Operator issues a time-critical command
analysis_records.response_measure: End-to-end response time < 200ms
architectural_decisions: Use of CORBA for remote object invocation
Distributed object model
analysis_records.reasoning: CORBA introduces overhead from marshaling/demarshaling, network traversal, and ORB processing. Achieving a hard 200ms deadline depends heavily on network latency, ORB implementation performance, and message size. Without real-time ORB extensions, non-deterministic garbage collection or thread scheduling can cause latency spikes.

risks.description: CORBA middleware overhead may violate the 200ms response time requirement under load or with large messages.
risks.rationale: Standard CORBA ORBs are not inherently real-time; marshaling, IIOP protocol processing, and location transparency add latency.

risks.description: Network congestion or latency between command center and remote sensor could dominate response time.
risks.rationale: CORBA does not control underlying network QoS. WAN links may have variable latency exceeding the budget.

non_risks.description: The distributed object model provides a clear, location-transparent path for the command invocation.
non_risks.rationale: The architectural pattern directly supports the remote operation stimulus.

scenario_reference.text: The system must operate continuously despite a partial network failure.

analysis_records.stimulus: Network link or node failure
analysis_records.response_measure: Core functions remain in degraded mode
architectural_decisions: Distributed Objects over a network
CORBA as communication middleware
analysis_records.reasoning: CORBA itself does not provide inherent fault tolerance for network partitions. Availability depends on higher-level system design: redundancy of components, failover mechanisms, and possibly replicated CORBA naming/services. The ORB may treat network failures as remote exceptions, potentially crashing clients if not handled.

risks.description: Single points of failure in CORBA services (e.g., Naming Service, Event Service) can bring down dependent components during a network partition.
risks.rationale: Core CORBA services are often centralized. Their failure disrupts object discovery and communication.

risks.description: The system may not gracefully degrade if critical remote objects become unreachable due to network failure.
risks.rationale: Clients may block or fail if they cannot locate or invoke remote objects, unless explicit timeout and fallback logic is implemented.

non_risks.description: Distribution itself allows for geographic redundancy of components.
non_risks.rationale: The architectural style does not preclude deploying redundant instances across different network segments.

scenario_reference.text: A legacy data processor is deprecated and needs replacement.

analysis_records.stimulus: Need to replace a legacy component
analysis_records.response_measure: Replacement within one week
architectural_decisions: Interface definition via CORBA IDL
Decoupling through standardized protocols
analysis_records.reasoning: The IDL defines a clear interface contract. If the new processor implements the same IDL interface, it can theoretically be swapped in. The one-week timeline assumes the new component's internal logic can be developed/tested independently and that integration is primarily about deployment and configuration.

risks.description: Legacy component may have implicit dependencies or side-effects not captured in the IDL, causing integration issues.
risks.rationale: IDL captures functional interface but not all behavioral semantics or environmental assumptions.

non_risks.description: The IDL provides a stable, versioned interface that shields the rest of the system from the component's internal changes.
non_risks.rationale: This is a core benefit of the interface-based decoupling pattern.

sensitivity_points.parameter: IDL Interface Stability and Backward Compatibility

scenario_reference.text: An external actor attempts to gain unauthorized access to the command channel.

analysis_records.stimulus: Unauthorized access attempt
analysis_records.response_measure: Attempt logged and blocked without disrupting authorized ops
architectural_decisions: CORBA as communication middleware
analysis_records.reasoning: Basic CORBA does not include security; it relies on the CORBA Security Service (CSS) or external mechanisms (e.g., TLS, firewalls). The ability to log and block without disruption depends on the performance and configuration of these security layers. If CSS is used, it may add significant overhead.

risks.description: CORBA IIOP traffic may be unencrypted by default, exposing commands to eavesdropping or tampering.
risks.rationale: Standard IIOP does not mandate encryption. Security is an add-on service.

risks.description: Security enforcement (authentication/authorization) could become a performance bottleneck or single point of failure.
risks.rationale: Centralized security services can be attacked or overloaded, affecting legitimate operations.

non_risks.description: The CORBA specification includes a Security Service specification for implementing security.
non_risks.rationale: A standardized framework exists to address security concerns, though its implementation is optional.

architectural_approaches.description: The system employs Common Object Request Broker Architecture (CORBA) as the middleware foundation to enable distributed object communication across heterogeneous components in ground-based command and control systems. This approach standardizes interfaces and facilitates location-transparent component integration.

addressed_attributes.rationale: CORBA provides language-independent and platform-independent interface definitions (IDL), enabling heterogeneous components from different vendors to communicate seamlessly regardless of implementation technology.

The focus on interface standardization rather than direct component reuse allows components to be replaced or modified independently as long as they conform to the defined interfaces, supporting plug-and-play integration.

CORBA middleware can be configured to support real-time performance requirements through priority-based request handling and deterministic communication patterns, though this requires careful design of the distributed object interactions.

architectural_approaches.description: The architecture mandates object-oriented technology as a foundational principle, promoting encapsulation, abstraction, and interface-based design to structure system components and their interactions.

addressed_attributes.rationale: Object-oriented principles such as encapsulation and separation of interface from implementation enable localized changes and reduce ripple effects across the system when modifications are needed.
Well-defined object interfaces provide clear contracts for component interaction, facilitating integration of components developed by different organizations.

architectural_approaches.description: The system serves as a reference architecture that defines standardized interfaces and common infrastructure patterns to be reused across multiple command and control system implementations, promoting strategic reuse.

addressed_attributes.rationale: By establishing a common architectural template, the reference architecture enables consistent modification patterns across multiple system instances and reduces the cost of evolving the architecture over time.
Standardized interfaces across the reference architecture ensure that systems built using this architecture can interoperate with each other and share components more easily.
