scenario_reference.text: A system integrator incorporates a new vendor component into the system using CORBA IDL interfaces. The integration must complete in less than 8 hours for IDL-compliant components with zero interface modifications required to existing components and successful interoperability test completion.

analysis_records.environment: Normal operations during system integration phase
analysis_records.stimulus: New vendor component with CORBA IDL interface requires integration
analysis_records.response_measure: Integration time < 8 hours, zero interface modifications to existing components, successful interoperability test completion
architectural_decisions: Use of CORBA IDL for language-independent and platform-independent interface definitions
Standardized reference architecture pattern enforcing interface contracts
Object-oriented encapsulation separating interface from implementation
analysis_records.reasoning: CORBA IDL provides a standardized contract mechanism that enables heterogeneous components to integrate without source-level dependencies. The reference architecture ensures consistent interface patterns across vendors. If the new component strictly adheres to published IDL specifications, integration involves only ORB configuration and interface binding, not code modification. The 8-hour target is achievable for IDL-compliant components through automated stub/skeleton generation and standardized deployment procedures.

risks.description: Vendor component may have undocumented dependencies on specific CORBA ORB implementations or versions
risks.rationale: CORBA standard allows vendor-specific extensions. If the new component relies on proprietary ORB features not present in the existing infrastructure, integration will require ORB upgrades or middleware reconfiguration, exceeding the 8-hour target.

risks.description: Semantic mismatches in IDL interface interpretation between vendors
risks.rationale: While IDL defines syntactic interfaces, semantic behavior (e.g., error handling, state management, transaction semantics) may differ between vendor implementations, causing interoperability failures despite syntactic compliance.

non_risks.description: Interface modifications to existing components are not required for IDL-compliant integration
non_risks.rationale: The architectural decision to use CORBA IDL as the integration contract ensures that existing components remain unchanged as long as the new component conforms to published interfaces. The ORB handles marshaling and protocol translation transparently.

sensitivity_points.parameter: IDL interface complexity (number of operations, parameter types)
Degree of CORBA standard compliance vs. vendor extensions

conflicting_attributes: Interoperability (positive: coarse-grained interfaces reduce integration points)
Performance (negative: coarse-grained interfaces increase message size and marshaling overhead)

scenario_reference.text: The system must operate continuously despite a partial network failure affecting CORBA communication paths. System uptime must be greater than or equal to 99.5%, with recovery time less than 30 seconds for non-critical services and less than 5 seconds for critical command paths, ensuring graceful degradation with no data loss.

analysis_records.environment: Operational system under partial network failure conditions
analysis_records.stimulus: Network partition or link failure disrupting CORBA communication between distributed components
analysis_records.response_measure: System uptime ≥ 99.5%, recovery time < 30s for non-critical services, < 5s for critical command paths, graceful degradation with no data loss
architectural_decisions: CORBA middleware for distributed object communication
Component-based architecture enabling independent failure domains
Object-oriented encapsulation supporting redundancy and failover mechanisms
analysis_records.reasoning: Achieving 99.5% uptime (43.8 hours downtime/year) with sub-5-second recovery for critical paths requires redundant communication paths, stateless or replicated component design, and rapid failure detection. CORBA itself does not inherently provide fault tolerance; the architecture must layer additional mechanisms (e.g., CORBA Fault Tolerant extensions, application-level heartbeats, redundant ORBs) on top of the middleware. The 5-second recovery target for critical commands demands pre-established backup paths and hot standby components to avoid connection re-establishment overhead.

risks.description: CORBA request timeout and exception handling may exceed 5-second recovery target for critical paths
risks.rationale: Standard CORBA timeout mechanisms and connection re-establishment can take 10-30 seconds depending on ORB configuration. Without pre-configured failover paths and aggressive timeout tuning, critical command recovery will violate the 5-second requirement.

risks.description: Stateful CORBA objects may lose state during failover, violating no-data-loss requirement
risks.rationale: If components maintain session state in CORBA object instances without persistent storage or state replication, network failures causing object migration or restart will result in state loss, contradicting the no-data-loss guarantee.

risks.description: Cascading failures due to synchronous CORBA invocation blocking
risks.rationale: Synchronous CORBA calls can cause thread exhaustion and cascading timeouts if failed components do not respond quickly. Without circuit breaker patterns or asynchronous messaging for non-critical paths, partial failures may propagate system-wide.

non_risks.description: Component isolation prevents total system failure from single component crashes
non_risks.rationale: The distributed object architecture with well-defined IDL interfaces creates natural failure boundaries. A single component failure affects only its direct clients, not the entire system, supporting graceful degradation.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Network redundancy topology (number of alternate paths)

conflicting_attributes: Availability (positive: shorter timeouts enable faster failover)
Reliability (negative: aggressive timeouts cause false positives under transient load)
Availability (positive: frequent replication reduces data loss)
Performance (negative: replication overhead increases latency and network traffic)

scenario_reference.text: Replace existing CORBA component with updated version maintaining IDL interface compatibility. Replacement time must be less than 4 hours, affecting no more than 2 directly dependent components, with no changes to IDL interfaces and full regression test suite passing.

analysis_records.stimulus: Developer replaces CORBA component implementation while preserving IDL interface
analysis_records.response_measure: Replacement time < 4 hours, affects ≤ 2 directly dependent components, no IDL changes, regression tests pass
architectural_decisions: CORBA IDL interface contracts separating specification from implementation
Object-oriented encapsulation hiding implementation details
Reference architecture standardizing component deployment patterns
analysis_records.reasoning: The architectural commitment to interface stability through CORBA IDL enables component replacement without ripple effects. If the new implementation maintains behavioral compatibility (not just syntactic IDL compliance), only the replaced component and its direct clients require testing. The 4-hour window accommodates component shutdown, deployment, ORB re-registration, and focused regression testing. The constraint of affecting ≤2 dependent components indicates low coupling, achievable through coarse-grained interfaces and minimal direct dependencies.

risks.description: Behavioral changes in component implementation may break client assumptions despite IDL compatibility
risks.rationale: IDL defines only syntactic contracts (method signatures, data types). If the new implementation changes timing behavior, error handling semantics, or side effects, clients relying on previous behavior will fail even though interfaces are unchanged.

non_risks.description: Interface stability prevents widespread system impact from component replacement
non_risks.rationale: The architectural decision to enforce strict IDL interface versioning ensures that component replacements maintaining interface compatibility require no changes to other system components. The ORB handles dynamic binding transparently.

non_risks.description: Regression test automation enables rapid validation within 4-hour window
non_risks.rationale: The reference architecture's standardized testing patterns and component isolation allow focused regression testing of the replaced component and its direct dependents, making the 4-hour target achievable.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Regression test suite coverage and execution time

conflicting_attributes: Modifiability (positive: stable interfaces reduce change impact)
Performance (negative: stable coarse interfaces may require inefficient workarounds for new features)

scenario_reference.text: Process critical command under normal load through CORBA middleware with priority-based request handling. End-to-end latency must be less than 100ms for critical commands and less than 500ms for standard commands, with deterministic response under peak load of 1000 requests per second.

analysis_records.environment: Normal operational load with peak traffic of 1000 requests/sec
analysis_records.stimulus: Critical command issued requiring priority processing through CORBA middleware
analysis_records.response_measure: End-to-end latency < 100ms for critical commands, < 500ms for standard commands, deterministic response under 1000 req/sec peak load
architectural_decisions: CORBA middleware with priority-based request handling configuration
Distributed object architecture enabling parallel processing
Real-time CORBA extensions for deterministic scheduling
analysis_records.reasoning: Achieving sub-100ms latency for critical commands through CORBA middleware requires careful attention to marshaling overhead, network latency, ORB scheduling, and server-side processing. At 1000 req/sec system-wide load, priority mechanisms must prevent lower-priority requests from blocking critical commands. Real-time CORBA (RT-CORBA) features like priority propagation, thread pools with priority lanes, and explicit binding can provide determinism. However, standard CORBA implementations may introduce 20-50ms overhead per remote call from marshaling, network transmission, and demarshaling, leaving limited budget for application logic.

risks.description: CORBA marshaling and network overhead may consume majority of 100ms latency budget
risks.rationale: Typical CORBA round-trip times range from 20-50ms on LAN depending on message complexity and ORB implementation. With multi-hop distributed object calls, cumulative middleware overhead can exceed the 100ms budget before application processing begins.

risks.description: Priority inversion in CORBA ORB thread pools under high load
risks.rationale: Without RT-CORBA priority propagation and careful thread pool configuration, high-priority critical commands may queue behind low-priority standard requests, causing unpredictable latency spikes that violate the 100ms guarantee.

risks.description: Non-deterministic garbage collection pauses in ORB runtime
risks.rationale: Many CORBA ORB implementations run on JVM or use garbage-collected languages. GC pauses of 50-200ms can occur unpredictably under load, violating real-time determinism requirements for critical commands.

non_risks.description: Distributed architecture enables parallel processing to handle 1000 req/sec throughput
non_risks.rationale: The distributed object model allows horizontal scaling by deploying multiple component instances across nodes. With proper load distribution, 1000 req/sec is achievable without saturating individual components.

sensitivity_points.parameter: CORBA message size and marshaling complexity
ORB thread pool size and priority configuration
Number of distributed object hops in critical command path

tradeoff_points.parameter: CORBA interface granularity for critical commands
conflicting_attributes: Real-time Performance (positive: coarse interfaces reduce remote calls and cumulative latency)
Modifiability (negative: coarse interfaces reduce flexibility and increase coupling)

tradeoff_points.parameter: Priority queue depth for critical commands
conflicting_attributes: Real-time Performance (positive: dedicated priority lanes ensure low latency)
Throughput (negative: reserved resources reduce capacity for standard requests)

scenario_reference.text: Unauthorized user attempts to invoke privileged CORBA operation on command component. Access must be denied within 50ms, security violation logged, with no system state corruption and complete audit trail maintained.

analysis_records.environment: Operational system with active authentication and authorization infrastructure
analysis_records.stimulus: Unauthorized user attempts to invoke privileged CORBA method
analysis_records.response_measure: Access denied within 50ms, security violation logged, no state corruption, complete audit trail
architectural_decisions: CORBA security service integration for authentication and authorization
Object-oriented encapsulation protecting component internal state
Centralized security policy enforcement at ORB interceptor level
analysis_records.reasoning: The 50ms access denial requirement demands efficient security checks, likely implemented as CORBA portable interceptors that validate credentials before method dispatch. This approach prevents unauthorized code execution while maintaining low overhead. Logging and audit trail generation must be asynchronous to avoid blocking the denial response. State corruption prevention relies on the security check occurring before any component logic executes, which CORBA request interceptors naturally provide.

risks.description: Synchronous audit logging may cause 50ms response time violation
risks.rationale: If security violation logging is performed synchronously (writing to database or file system before returning denial), I/O latency can easily exceed 50ms, especially under high load or storage contention.

risks.description: Distributed security credential validation may introduce network round-trips exceeding 50ms budget
risks.rationale: If authorization decisions require remote calls to centralized policy servers or LDAP directories, network latency and server processing time can exceed the 50ms target, especially in geographically distributed deployments.

non_risks.description: CORBA interceptor architecture prevents state corruption from unauthorized access
non_risks.rationale: Security checks implemented as CORBA portable interceptors execute before method dispatch, ensuring that unauthorized requests never reach component logic. This architectural decision guarantees no state corruption from failed access attempts.

non_risks.description: Object encapsulation limits blast radius of security breaches
non_risks.rationale: The object-oriented architecture with well-defined interfaces ensures that even if an attacker bypasses one component's security, they cannot directly access internal state of other components, limiting lateral movement.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Security policy complexity (number of rules evaluated)

conflicting_attributes: Security (positive: fine-grained checks provide better access control)
Performance (negative: more checks increase latency and overhead)
Security (positive: detailed logs improve forensics and compliance)
Performance (negative: verbose logging increases I/O overhead and storage requirements)

scenarios.scenario_text: A developer needs to reuse the Event Manager, Event Queue, and Handler Registry components in a new application domain without modifying the core framework code.

A new event type is introduced to the system. A developer registers a new event handler through the Handler Registry without changing the Event Manager or Event Queue implementation, completing the modification within 2 hours.

The framework must accommodate a new business requirement for priority-based event handling. The modification is implemented by extending the event dispatching mechanism with minimal impact to existing handlers.
During normal operation, the Event Queue receives 100 events in rapid succession. The system processes all events in FIFO order without dropping or reordering any events.

A user submits an invalid event object (missing required fields) to the Event Manager. The system detects the invalid input, logs an error, and continues processing subsequent valid events without crashing or entering an inconsistent state.

A new developer joins the project and must understand the event flow from event submission to handler execution. The consistent event-driven paradigm allows the developer to trace the architecture within 4 hours of onboarding.

All framework components (Event Manager, Event Queue, Handler Registry) interact exclusively through the event dispatching mechanism, maintaining architectural coherence and preventing direct component coupling.

Under normal load conditions (50 events per second), the Event Manager dispatches events to registered handlers with an average latency of less than 10 milliseconds from queue insertion to handler invocation.

evaluation_inputs.system_description: MINPHIS is a service-oriented health information system designed specifically for the Nigerian and African healthcare context. Originally based on MUMPS language, FileMan-database, and Kernel-package, the system has undergone modernization to a Client-Server architecture utilizing an RPC Broker. It serves as a low-cost, sustainable application for managing patient records, accounting, and medical records across federal, state, and local government healthcare tiers.

risks.rationale: The RPC communication adds network round-trip time. Without guaranteed low-latency/high-bandwidth network, the response time goal is at risk.

risks.rationale: A single server (or cluster) handling all business logic is a potential bottleneck. Performance depends on unspecified hardware specs and concurrent user load.

non_risks.description: The RPC Broker provides a structured, efficient mechanism for remote procedure calls, which is a suitable pattern for request-response transactions like order submission.
non_risks.rationale: RPC is a standard, well-understood pattern for client-server communication, facilitating predictable interaction.

scenario_reference.text: The system maintains 99.9% availability during core clinic hours (8 AM-6 PM).

analysis_records.environment: Normal business operations during core hours

analysis_records.response_measure: System uptime of 99.9% (approx. 43.2 minutes of downtime per month allowed)
architectural_decisions: Server-side management of critical logic and data
Potential for server clustering (implied by Availability scenario A1)
analysis_records.reasoning: 99.9% availability is a demanding target. The reliability of the single server (or cluster) is critical. The architecture's reliability hinges on server hardware robustness, software stability, and operational procedures (e.g., patching, backups).

risks.description: Single server deployment (if not clustered) creates a single point of failure, making 99.9% availability difficult to achieve.
risks.rationale: Any hardware failure, OS crash, or required maintenance on the primary server causes total system downtime.

risks.description: The RPC Broker component itself could be a single point of failure if not designed for high availability.
risks.rationale: If the broker fails, all client-server communication halts.

non_risks.description: Centralizing business logic on the server simplifies monitoring and health checks for the core system component.
non_risks.rationale: A single, well-instrumented server is easier to monitor for reliability metrics than distributed logic.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Mean Time Between Failures (MTBF) of server hardware
Planned maintenance window duration and frequency

scenario_reference.text: The server component fails; a clustered backup server takes over within 30 seconds with no data loss.

analysis_records.stimulus: Primary server hardware or software failure
analysis_records.response_measure: Backup server takes over within 30 seconds with no data loss
architectural_decisions: Server clustering for high availability
Use of shared or replicated data storage
analysis_records.reasoning: This scenario explicitly tests the failover capability. The 30-second Recovery Time Objective (RTO) and zero data loss (RPO=0) are stringent. The architecture must include a robust clustering mechanism with synchronous data replication and fast failure detection.

risks.description: Achieving a 30-second failover with no data loss requires synchronous replication and instant failure detection, which is complex and may impact performance.
risks.rationale: Synchronous replication adds latency to primary server writes. Slow failure detection can breach the 30-second RTO.

risks.description: The RPC Broker must be cluster-aware to redirect client connections to the new active server within the failover time.
risks.rationale: If clients remain connected to the failed server's broker endpoint, service is interrupted until they reconnect.

non_risks.description: The Client-Server model naturally supports active-passive or active-active clustering patterns for the server component.
non_risks.rationale: The architecture separates client and server, allowing the server layer to be replaced without changing clients, given proper broker redirection.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Data replication latency between primary and backup servers

evaluation_inputs.system_description: A large-scale health care system (millions of lines of code) designed to serve as an information backbone for hospitals, clinics, and HMOs. It consists of two major subsystems: the OnLine Transaction Manager (OLTM) for interactive tasks and the Decision Support and Report Generation Manager (DSRGM) for batch processing. scenario_reference.text: A rule in the rule engine fires, and data access must complete within 2 seconds.

analysis_records.stimulus: Rule engine fires, triggering data access request.
analysis_records.response_measure: Data access latency < 2s
architectural_decisions: Use of a layered architecture separating rule engine, business logic, and data access.
Integration of COTS rule engine and database components.
Implementation of caching at the business logic or data access layer.
analysis_records.reasoning: The layered architecture introduces network hops between components, which can increase latency. COTS components may have non-optimized data access paths. Caching can mitigate latency for frequently accessed data but adds complexity.

risks.description: Network latency between the rule engine layer and the data source layer may cause the 2-second threshold to be exceeded, especially if data is not co-located.
risks.rationale: The layered architecture inherently adds communication overhead. Without low-latency network links and efficient query design, response time may suffer.

risks.description: The COTS rule engine or database may have performance limitations under high load, causing slow data retrieval.
risks.rationale: COTS components are generic and may not be optimized for the specific data access patterns of the rule engine, leading to unpredictable performance.

non_risks.description: Separation of concerns via layers localizes performance tuning to the data access layer.
non_risks.rationale: The layered style allows optimization of the data access layer (e.g., query optimization, indexing) without affecting the rule engine logic, reducing risk of widespread changes.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Network round-trip time between application server and database

scenario_reference.text: Data in the information hub is replicated to a branch clinic; system performance (e.g., response time) degrades by no more than 20%.

analysis_records.stimulus: Initiation of data replication process from information hub to branch clinic.
analysis_records.response_measure: System performance degradation <= 20% of baseline response time.
architectural_decisions: Use of asynchronous replication to decouple primary operations from replication tasks.
Allocation of separate network bandwidth or dedicated replication servers.
Layered isolation where replication logic resides in a separate service layer.
analysis_records.reasoning: Asynchronous replication reduces immediate impact on user transactions but may consume shared resources (CPU, I/O, network). Dedicated resources help but increase cost. Layered isolation can contain the performance impact to specific layers.

risks.description: Replication process consumes significant I/O bandwidth on the shared database server, causing contention and slowing down primary user transactions.
risks.rationale: If replication is not properly throttled or uses the same data storage layer, it can directly compete with operational data access, leading to >20% degradation.

non_risks.description: Asynchronous replication design prevents replication latency from blocking user requests.
non_risks.rationale: By decoupling the replication flow from the main transaction path, the user-facing layers can maintain responsiveness even if replication lags.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Available I/O throughput on the database server

conflicting_attributes: Performance (Async reduces impact on primary operations)
Data Consistency (Async may lead to temporary data staleness)

scenario_reference.text: Previously public data is made private, and access rules are adjusted; the change is implemented and deployed within one person-day of effort.

analysis_records.environment: Normal operations, during a change window
analysis_records.stimulus: Business requirement change to data privacy/access rules.
analysis_records.response_measure: Change implemented and deployed within 1 person-day.
architectural_decisions: Centralized access control logic within a dedicated security/authorization layer.
Use of declarative, configuration-based rule definitions (potentially via a COTS security component).
Layered separation ensuring data privacy changes are confined to the business logic and security layers.
analysis_records.reasoning: A centralized, configurable security layer allows rule changes without code modifications. The layered architecture isolates changes, preventing ripple effects to presentation or data layers. COTS security components may offer rapid reconfiguration.

risks.description: Access rules are hard-coded or scattered across multiple application modules, requiring extensive code changes and testing.
risks.rationale: If the architecture does not centralize security policy, a simple rule change could necessitate modifications in many places, exceeding the 1-day effort limit.

non_risks.description: Layered architecture with a dedicated security service localizes the change impact.
non_risks.rationale: The change is confined to the security layer's configuration or service logic, minimizing testing and deployment scope.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Granularity and complexity of the access control policy model

conflicting_attributes: Modifiability (improved, as changes are in one place)
Performance (may add latency due to extra authorization calls)

scenario_reference.text: A new, better COTS component becomes available; the system can integrate it with changes isolated primarily to the business logic layer, causing less than 4 hours of downtime.

analysis_records.stimulus: Availability of a new, superior COTS component for integration.
analysis_records.response_measure: Integration completed with changes primarily in business logic layer and < 4 hours downtime.
architectural_decisions: Strict layer encapsulation with well-defined interfaces between business logic and COTS components.
Use of adapter/wrapper patterns to abstract COTS-specific APIs.
Dependency injection or service locator patterns to allow runtime component swapping where possible.
analysis_records.reasoning: Well-defined interfaces and abstraction patterns minimize the impact of swapping a COTS component. However, if the new component's interface or semantics differ significantly, the adapter layer may require substantial changes, potentially affecting other layers. Downtime is primarily for deployment and data migration.

risks.description: Tight coupling between business logic and the specific COTS component's proprietary API, requiring extensive rewrites beyond the business logic layer.
risks.rationale: Without a clean abstraction layer, replacing the COTS component may necessitate changes in data models, presentation logic, or even other integrated systems, increasing downtime and effort.

non_risks.description: Use of adapter pattern and dependency injection confines integration changes to the component wrapper and configuration.
non_risks.rationale: The core business logic interacts with a stable interface; only the adapter implementing that interface for the new COTS needs to be changed, limiting scope.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Stability and completeness of the abstract interface definition for the COTS functionality

tradeoff_points.parameter: Level of abstraction over COTS components

scenario_reference.text: An external actor attempts to access private patient data; the system detects and logs the attempt within 5 minutes, preventing data breach.

analysis_records.stimulus: Unauthorized access attempt to private patient data.
analysis_records.response_measure: Attempt detected and logged within 5 minutes; data breach prevented.
architectural_decisions: Implementation of a centralized audit logging service (potentially a COTS SIEM or logging component).
Integration of intrusion detection mechanisms at network and application layers.
Strict access control enforcement at each layer (presentation, business logic, data).
analysis_records.reasoning: Centralized logging enables correlation and timely detection. Layered security provides defense in depth. However, detection latency depends on log aggregation speed and analysis rule efficiency. COTS security components may offer out-of-the-box detection but require proper configuration.

risks.description: Logs are generated but not monitored in real-time; detection relies on manual review, causing delays beyond 5 minutes.
risks.rationale: Without automated log analysis and alerting, even a well-logged event may not be noticed promptly, failing the detection time requirement.

non_risks.description: Layered architecture allows access control checks at multiple points (e.g., API gateway, business service, database), increasing chances of blocking unauthorized access early.
non_risks.rationale: An attempt blocked at the presentation layer gateway may never reach business logic or data, simplifying detection and prevention.

tradeoff_points.parameter: Granularity and volume of security logging

scenario_reference.text: User base grows by 50%; the system scales by adding application servers to the business logic layer, maintaining response times within 10% of baseline.

analysis_records.stimulus: 50% increase in concurrent users.
analysis_records.response_measure: Response times maintained within 10% of baseline via horizontal scaling of business logic layer.
architectural_decisions: Stateless design of business logic components to enable horizontal scaling.
Use of a load balancer in front of the business logic layer.
Layered separation allowing independent scaling of the business logic tier.
analysis_records.reasoning: Statelessness is key for linear scaling. The load balancer distributes traffic. The layered architecture allows scaling the business logic layer without necessarily scaling presentation or data layers. However, the shared data layer (database) may become a bottleneck.

risks.description: The database layer becomes a bottleneck under increased load, preventing the business logic layer from maintaining response times despite scaling.
risks.rationale: Scaling the application servers increases database connection pools and query load. If the database is not also scaled or optimized, response times will degrade beyond 10%.

non_risks.description: Stateless business logic components allow new application servers to be added seamlessly to the load-balanced pool.
non_risks.rationale: No user session affinity is required, so traffic distribution is efficient, supporting linear scaling for the business logic layer itself.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Database connection pool size and query throughput

scenario_reference.text: The system is deployed in a new region with a different language and currency; administrators configure these via settings, requiring no software deployment or downtime.

analysis_records.environment: System expansion to a new geographical region
analysis_records.stimulus: Need to support new regional settings (language, currency).
analysis_records.response_measure: Configuration via admin settings, zero deployment/downtime.
architectural_decisions: Externalization of all locale-specific strings and formats (like currency symbols) to resource files or a configuration database.
Presentation layer designed to dynamically load locale resources based on user or system settings.
Use of COTS localization libraries or frameworks.
analysis_records.reasoning: Externalizing configuration separates regional concerns from code. The layered architecture allows the presentation layer to adapt without changes to business logic or data layers. COTS libraries may simplify implementation but must support dynamic reconfiguration.

risks.description: Locale-specific logic (e.g., date formatting, currency calculations) is embedded in business logic code, requiring code changes and redeployment.
risks.rationale: If internationalization is not fully externalized, a new region may require modifications to core business rules, violating the 'no deployment' requirement.

non_risks.description: Layered architecture confines localization changes to the presentation layer and external resource files.
non_risks.rationale: Business logic and data layers remain unchanged; only configuration files for the new locale need to be added and activated by administrators.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Completeness of internationalization (i18n) coverage in the codebase

tradeoff_points.parameter: Dynamic vs. static locale resource loading
conflicting_attributes: Performance (May increase initial page load time)

scenario_reference.text: Performance degrades during data replication; operations team uses system monitoring/logging to identify the bottleneck and resolve it within 2 hours.

analysis_records.stimulus: Performance degradation observed during data replication.
analysis_records.response_measure: Bottleneck identified and resolved within 2 hours using monitoring/logging.
architectural_decisions: Comprehensive, centralized logging and metrics collection across all layers.
Use of COTS application performance monitoring (APM) and log aggregation tools.
Layered instrumentation to isolate metrics per component (e.g., database I/O, network latency, business logic execution time).
analysis_records.reasoning: Centralized monitoring with layer-specific metrics enables rapid root cause isolation. COTS APM tools can provide out-of-the-box dashboards and alerts. However, if logging is insufficient or metrics are too coarse, diagnosis may take longer than 2 hours.

risks.description: Monitoring lacks granular metrics for the replication process itself (e.g., replication queue length, network throughput to branch), delaying identification of the specific bottleneck.
risks.rationale: Without detailed metrics for the replication subsystem, operations must rely on generic system metrics (CPU, memory), which may not pinpoint the cause, extending diagnosis time.

non_risks.description: Layered architecture allows monitoring agents to be deployed per layer, providing clear segmentation of performance data.
non_risks.rationale: Operations can quickly determine if degradation is in the data layer (high I/O), network layer (high latency), or application layer (high CPU), narrowing the search.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Alert threshold sensitivity and correlation rules in the monitoring system

scenario_reference.text: The system must send patient treatment records to an external regional healthcare registry using a standard HL7/FHIR interface, successfully completing the exchange for 99% of records.

analysis_records.environment: Normal operations, during data exchange batches
analysis_records.stimulus: Requirement to send patient treatment records to an external registry.
analysis_records.response_measure: 99% successful exchange completion using standard HL7/FHIR interface.
architectural_decisions: Implementation of a dedicated integration layer (e.g., Enterprise Service Bus - ESB) or adapter for protocol translation.
Use of COTS healthcare integration engines supporting HL7/FHIR standards.
Layered isolation where integration logic is separate from core business logic.
analysis_records.reasoning: A dedicated integration layer handles protocol specifics, transformation, and error handling. COTS integration engines reduce custom code. The layered style prevents interoperability concerns from polluting core business logic. Success rate depends on network reliability, data quality, and external system availability.

risks.description: External registry's HL7/FHIR implementation may have non-standard extensions or validation rules, causing message rejections and lowering success rate below 99%.
risks.rationale: Even with standards, interoperability often requires custom mapping and testing. Without a flexible adapter, message failures may be frequent.

non_risks.description: Use of a COTS integration engine with built-in HL7/FHIR connectors reduces development effort and leverages proven interoperability features.
non_risks.rationale: COTS components are often certified for standards compliance and include error handling and retry mechanisms, increasing likelihood of successful exchange.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Network reliability and latency between the system and the external registry

tradeoff_points.parameter: Coupling between business logic and external interface
conflicting_attributes: Interoperability (Loose coupling via integration layer improves adaptability)
Performance (Additional hop through integration layer may add latency)

analysis_records.reasoning: The decentralized approach eliminates a single point of failure and potential bottleneck of a central server, which could improve responsiveness. However, distributed decision-making among 50 agents introduces coordination overhead (e.g., message passing for task discovery, negotiation, conflict resolution). Without quantitative data on network latency, message size, and agent processing time, the 5-second target is an architectural assumption. The risk is that under high load, the consensus or negotiation process may exceed the latency target.

analysis_records.reasoning: The agent-based architecture and middleware abstraction layer promote flexibility. New AGV models can be integrated by implementing a standard agent interface that communicates with the middleware. The one-week target is feasible if the middleware provides clear APIs and the new AGV's capabilities can be modeled within the existing agent protocol. risks.rationale: The openness scenario (O1) targets protocol heterogeneity, but if the middleware lacks a plugin for the new protocol, significant development effort is required.

non_risks.rationale: As long as the new AGV can implement the standard agent interface and communicate via a supported protocol, integration is primarily a configuration and testing exercise.

risks.description: Semantic mismatches between different protocol message formats may cause information loss or errors during translation.
risks.rationale: Protocols like MQTT (pub/sub) and ROS (services/topics) have different communication paradigms. Faithful translation of complex messages (e.g., containing route plans) is non-trivial.

risks.rationale: While the agent coordination is decentralized, all cross-protocol messages must pass through the middleware for translation, creating a centralized choke point.

non_risks.description: The use of a dedicated middleware layer isolates protocol-specific code, making it easier to add new protocol adapters in the future.
non_risks.rationale: The architecture explicitly separates concerns, which is a sound practice for achieving openness.

scenarios.scenario_text: During normal warehouse operations with up to 140 transports per hour, AGVs receive transport task assignments and must route efficiently through the warehouse layout. The system must ensure that AGVs complete transports using paths within 10% of the optimal shortest route, maintaining the target throughput of 112-140 transports per hour.

During normal operations with up to 12 AGVs active and 140 transports per hour, multiple AGVs approach the same intersection simultaneously. The decentralized collision avoidance mechanism must coordinate AGV movements over the limited bandwidth network (11 Mbps) to ensure zero collisions occur, with all AGVs safely navigating intersections without central coordination.

During peak operations, AGVs executing multiple concurrent transports encounter a potential deadlock situation where circular dependencies in path reservations could halt operations. The system must detect the deadlock condition and resolve it within 30 seconds through decentralized negotiation, maintaining operational availability greater than 99% without requiring central arbitration.

During normal operations, a warehouse operator performs a controlled addition or removal of an AGV from the fleet (e.g., for maintenance or to scale capacity). The decentralized MAS architecture must detect the topology change, redistribute active transports if necessary, and continue operations with the remaining AGVs within 10 seconds, with zero transport failures and no manual reconfiguration required.

During operations, a transport task has been assigned to an AGV but has not yet been picked up. A more suitable AGV (closer proximity, better route efficiency) becomes available. The system must dynamically reassign the transport to the more suitable AGV within the reconsideration period (20-200 time steps) using the CNET protocol, while maintaining network bandwidth usage below the 60% threshold (6.6 Mbps of 11 Mbps total) to prevent communication failures.

A third-party AGV with different hardware specifications and control software needs to be integrated into the existing warehouse system. The decentralized MAS architecture must accommodate the new AGV through the virtual environment middleware interface, requiring less than 2 weeks of engineering effort and minimal custom middleware development, while maintaining compatibility with existing low-level Vehicle Control software and legacy libraries.

scenario_reference.text: During a virtual meeting, the network connection fails for a user and later recovers. The system should reconnect the user to the session without requiring a full restart.

analysis_records.environment: Network interruption during an active virtual meeting session.
analysis_records.stimulus: User's network connection fails and then recovers.
analysis_records.response_measure: User reconnects to the session automatically; session state is preserved.
architectural_decisions: Client-Server architecture for central session management.
Plugin/Module Architecture for the virtual meeting feature.
analysis_records.reasoning: The Client-Server style centralizes session state on the server, which is necessary for reconnection. However, the specific reconnection logic (heartbeats, timeouts, state persistence) is dependent on the implementation of the virtual meeting module (a plugin). Without details on this mechanism, the ability to meet the scenario is uncertain.

risks.description: The virtual meeting module may not implement robust session state persistence and automatic reconnection protocols.
risks.rationale: The Plugin/Module Architecture allows for variation in quality. If the module treats sessions as stateless or has short timeouts, users may be disconnected and unable to rejoin seamlessly.

non_risks.description: The central server remains available to manage reconnection requests.
non_risks.rationale: The Client-Server approach ensures a stable endpoint for clients to reconnect to after network recovery.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Session timeout duration in the virtual meeting module

tradeoff_points.parameter: Amount of session state persisted server-side

scenario_reference.text: A user enters an incorrect username and password combination. The system must deny access and not reveal whether the username exists.

analysis_records.stimulus: User submits invalid credentials.
analysis_records.response_measure: Access denied with a generic error message; no information leakage about username existence.
architectural_decisions: Layered Architecture (3-Tier)
Model-View-Controller (MVC)
analysis_records.reasoning: The Layered and MVC architectures separate presentation from business logic. This allows the application logic layer to implement a security control that returns a uniform error message regardless of whether the username is valid, preventing information disclosure. This is a standard and low-risk implementation.

non_risks.description: Architectural separation enforces a generic error response at the application logic layer.
non_risks.rationale: The tiered separation prevents the view/presentation layer from receiving or displaying detailed authentication failure reasons from the database layer.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Implementation correctness of the authentication logic

scenario_reference.text: A user sends an email containing sensitive grade information through the system. The email must be encapsulated and secured (e.g., encrypted).

analysis_records.stimulus: User sends an email with sensitive content.
analysis_records.response_measure: Email content is encrypted during transmission.
architectural_decisions: Client-Server architecture over HTTP/HTTPS.
analysis_records.reasoning: The Client-Server style relies on the underlying transport protocol (HTTPS/TLS) to provide channel encryption between client and server. This protects data in transit. However, end-to-end encryption or encryption at rest within the system is not guaranteed by this architecture alone.

risks.description: Lack of end-to-end encryption or encryption of data at rest within the server/mail queue.
risks.rationale: HTTPS only secures the client-server link. If the email is stored or processed in plaintext on the server or forwarded via an unencrypted channel to the final mail server, confidentiality could be breached.

non_risks.description: Transport-layer encryption (TLS/HTTPS) is enforced for client-server communication.
non_risks.rationale: Standard web deployment practice mandates HTTPS, which encrypts all data in transit between the user's browser and the Moodle server.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Email routing and storage configuration post-submission

scenario_reference.text: A user clicks an icon (e.g., to submit an assignment or load a course page) and expects the information to process and the page to update with speed (e.g., within 2 seconds).

analysis_records.stimulus: User initiates an action (click).
analysis_records.response_measure: Page updates within 2 seconds.
architectural_decisions: Layered Architecture (3-Tier)
Model-View-Controller (MVC)
Client-Server
analysis_records.reasoning: The multi-tier architecture introduces processing latency at each layer (presentation, application logic, database). The 2-second target is achievable under normal load but is sensitive to server performance, database query efficiency, and network latency. Without quantitative data on these parameters, performance is a potential risk area.

risks.description: Cascading latency through the layered tiers may cause response times to exceed 2 seconds under load or with inefficient queries.
risks.rationale: Each layer (web server, PHP application, database) adds processing time. Bottlenecks at any layer (e.g., slow database joins) directly impact end-to-end latency.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Application server (PHP) processing capacity and caching
Network latency between client and server

scenario_reference.text: A student downloads a set of lecture slides (e.g., a 50MB PDF file). The download should initiate promptly and complete within an acceptable time given the network bandwidth.

analysis_records.stimulus: User requests a large file download.
analysis_records.response_measure: Download completes within a time acceptable for the given network bandwidth.
architectural_decisions: Client-Server architecture.
Layered Architecture (presentation and application tiers).
analysis_records.reasoning: File downloads are typically served directly by the web server (presentation tier) or via the application tier. Performance is primarily governed by available network bandwidth and server I/O capacity. The architecture does not inherently introduce bottlenecks for static content delivery.

risks.description: Network bandwidth between the server and the client may be insufficient, causing unacceptable download times.
risks.rationale: The architecture does not mitigate fundamental network constraints. If the server is hosted on a low-bandwidth connection or the user has a poor connection, download performance will suffer.

non_risks.description: Static file serving can be optimized at the web server layer (presentation tier) without involving heavy application logic.
non_risks.rationale: The Layered Architecture allows large files to be served efficiently by the front-end web server (e.g., Apache, Nginx) using efficient protocols, minimizing load on the application tier.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Available network bandwidth (server uplink, client downlink)
Web server configuration for static content caching and compression

scenario_reference.text: A teacher wants to add new web pages to their course's wiki module to include updated learning materials. This should be possible without developer intervention.

analysis_records.stimulus: Teacher requests to add content to an existing wiki.
analysis_records.response_measure: Content can be added via the wiki's built-in editing interface.
architectural_decisions: Plugin/Module Architecture
Model-View-Controller (MVC)
analysis_records.reasoning: The wiki is implemented as a module. The MVC pattern within the module provides a user interface (View) for editing and a data model for storage. This scenario is a core function of the wiki module and is well-supported by the architecture, posing low risk.

non_risks.description: The wiki module, as a plugin, provides self-contained content management features accessible to teachers.
non_risks.rationale: The Plugin/Module Architecture is designed precisely for this: extending system functionality in a user-accessible way without touching core code. The MVC separation allows for a dedicated editing interface.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Wiki module's user permission and role configuration

risks.description: The external service ('mybox') may have API or authentication requirements that are incompatible or complex to implement within the Moodle plugin framework.
risks.rationale: While the architecture supports plugins, the difficulty of integration is determined by the external system's constraints, which may require significant custom development.

non_risks.description: The core system provides defined extension points (APIs, hooks) for file repository plugins.
non_risks.rationale: The Plugin/Module Architecture is explicitly designed to allow such integrations without modifying the core, fulfilling the basic requirement of the scenario.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Stability and documentation of Moodle's file repository plugin API
Complexity of the external service's authentication protocol (e.g., OAuth flow)

tradeoff_points.parameter: Depth of integration (full feature set vs. basic)

analysis_records.response_measure: System provides an error message and preserves other unsaved data; does not crash.
architectural_decisions: Model-View-Controller (MVC)
Layered Architecture (3-Tier)
analysis_records.reasoning: MVC separates validation logic (Controller/Model) from the user interface. Invalid input should be caught by the controller or model, with an error message returned to the view. The layered architecture helps contain errors within the application logic tier. Data preservation depends on client-side or server-side session management implementation.

risks.description: If validation logic is incomplete or the controller does not properly manage transaction state, a submission error could lead to partial data loss or an unstable state.
risks.rationale: While the architecture supports clean error handling, its effectiveness depends on the rigorous implementation of validation and state rollback within each module.

non_risks.description: The separation provided by MVC allows invalid input to be rejected before it affects core data models or causes system-level faults.
non_risks.rationale: The controller can validate input and return an error to the view without invoking model operations that could crash, supporting graceful degradation.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Robustness of input validation and sanitization routines
Client-side form state preservation (e.g., using JavaScript)

analysis_records.response_measure: Response time < 5 seconds for 95% of requests
architectural_decisions: Web-based Client-Server Architecture with centralized server-side processing
Server handles heavy file upload processing
Modular architecture isolates upload functionality
analysis_records.reasoning: The centralized server must handle concurrent file uploads efficiently. Without explicit load balancing, caching, or asynchronous processing mechanisms documented, the server becomes a bottleneck. Network bandwidth between clients and server, disk I/O capacity, and database connection pool size directly impact upload performance. The 5-second target for 100MB files requires minimum 20MB/s throughput per upload, which multiplied by concurrent users creates significant resource demands.

risks.description: Centralized server may become bottleneck under concurrent large file uploads without documented load balancing or horizontal scaling
risks.rationale: 500 concurrent users uploading 100MB files simultaneously could exceed server I/O capacity, network bandwidth, and memory resources, causing response times to exceed 5-second threshold

risks.description: Database connection pool exhaustion during concurrent upload metadata storage
risks.rationale: Each upload requires database transactions for metadata storage; insufficient connection pool size could cause queuing delays

risks.description: Network bandwidth saturation between distributed clients and centralized server
risks.rationale: 100MB uploads from 500 concurrent users require substantial bandwidth; internet/intranet capacity constraints not documented

non_risks.description: Module isolation prevents upload failures from affecting other system components
non_risks.rationale: Modular architecture ensures upload processing failures remain contained within the upload module

conflicting_attributes: Availability (larger buffers consume more memory, risking OOM failures)

risks.description: Authentication overhead on every content request may degrade performance
risks.rationale: If authentication validation occurs on each SCORM content request without session caching, cumulative overhead could exceed 2-second threshold

non_risks.description: SCORM standards compliance ensures predictable content structure and processing
non_risks.rationale: Standardized SCORM packaging allows optimized parsing and delivery mechanisms

Without documented redundancy, failover mechanisms, or high-availability clustering, hardware failures, network outages, or maintenance windows could exceed the downtime budget. Module isolation helps contain failures but doesn't address server-level availability.

risks.description: Centralized server represents single point of failure without documented redundancy
risks.rationale: Hardware failure, network outage, or datacenter issues could cause complete system unavailability exceeding 3.6-hour monthly budget

risks.description: Planned maintenance windows may consume entire downtime budget
risks.rationale: Software updates, security patches, and database maintenance require downtime; without hot-swap or rolling update capability, maintenance could exceed 99.5% target

risks.description: Internet/intranet network dependency creates external failure points
risks.rationale: ISP outages or network infrastructure failures outside system control could impact availability

non_risks.description: Module isolation prevents individual plugin failures from causing total system unavailability
non_risks.rationale: Modular architecture ensures core system remains available even if specific modules fail

analysis_records.stimulus: Unauthenticated user attempts to access protected resources
analysis_records.response_measure: 100% access blocking with redirect to login within 1 second
architectural_decisions: Authentication and Authorization Framework controlling resource access
Credential validation before granting access to main pages
Web-based architecture enforcing server-side authentication checks
analysis_records.reasoning: The authentication framework must intercept all requests to protected resources and validate credentials before allowing access. The 100% blocking requirement demands fail-secure design with no bypass vulnerabilities. The 1-second redirect constraint requires efficient authentication checks without complex cryptographic operations that could introduce latency.

risks.description: Authentication bypass vulnerabilities if framework not applied consistently across all protected endpoints
risks.rationale: Incomplete coverage of authentication checks could allow direct URL access to protected resources, violating 100% blocking requirement

risks.description: Session fixation or hijacking attacks if session management not properly implemented
risks.rationale: Weak session token generation or insecure transmission could allow attackers to impersonate authenticated users

non_risks.description: Server-side authentication enforcement prevents client-side bypass
non_risks.rationale: Web-based client-server architecture ensures authentication logic executes on trusted server, not manipulable client

non_risks.description: 1-second redirect constraint is achievable with standard authentication mechanisms
non_risks.rationale: Session token validation and redirect operations typically complete in milliseconds, well within 1-second budget

conflicting_attributes: Security (stronger cryptography improves resistance to attacks)
Performance (complex cryptographic operations increase validation latency)

scenario_reference.text: When authenticated users with insufficient privileges attempt to access restricted modules (assignments, forums, Turnitin), the authorization system denies access and logs the attempt within 500ms

analysis_records.stimulus: Authenticated user with insufficient privileges attempts module access

architectural_decisions: Authentication and Authorization Framework with role-based access control
Modular architecture with per-module authorization checks
Logging mechanism for security audit trails
analysis_records.reasoning: Authorization requires mapping user roles to module permissions and enforcing access control. The 500ms constraint demands efficient permission lookups, likely requiring cached role-permission mappings. Logging adds overhead but is critical for security auditing. The modular architecture requires consistent authorization enforcement across all plugin modules.

risks.description: Inconsistent authorization enforcement across plugin modules
risks.rationale: Plugin-based architecture may allow third-party modules to implement custom authorization logic, creating potential for privilege escalation vulnerabilities

risks.description: Authorization decision caching may serve stale permissions after role changes
risks.rationale: To meet 500ms constraint, permission lookups likely use caching; insufficient cache invalidation could allow access after privilege revocation

risks.description: Logging mechanism failure could prevent security audit trails
risks.rationale: If logging is synchronous and fails, it could either block the authorization decision or silently fail to record unauthorized access attempts

non_risks.description: 500ms response time is sufficient for role-based authorization checks
non_risks.rationale: Database lookups for user roles and permission mappings typically complete in tens of milliseconds, leaving margin for logging

conflicting_attributes: Performance (longer cache duration reduces database queries)
Security (shorter cache duration ensures timely permission revocation)
Performance (verbose logging increases I/O overhead and storage requirements)

architectural_decisions: Modular architecture with plugin isolation
Independent module execution contexts preventing cascading failures
Core system resilience to plugin failures
analysis_records.reasoning: Module isolation requires process-level separation, exception handling boundaries, or resource quotas to prevent failure propagation. The 'no degradation' requirement means other modules must maintain full functionality and performance despite the failed module. This demands careful design of inter-module communication and shared resource management.

risks.rationale: If module isolation doesn't include resource cleanup, crashed modules could leave allocated memory unreleased, eventually impacting system-wide performance

non_risks.description: Modular architecture design explicitly supports failure isolation
non_risks.rationale: Plugin-based architecture with module boundaries enables independent failure domains

evaluation_inputs.system_description: An online credit-card transaction system that receives credit information from terminals, delivers transaction requests to credit-card companies, and transmits responses back to terminals. It requires continuous 24/7 operation and real-time synchronization with backup systems and external databases.

analysis_records.stimulus: Hardware failure, software crash, or maintenance event
analysis_records.response_measure: System operational 24/7/365 (99.999% uptime target)
architectural_decisions: Use of redundant, load-balanced application servers
Use of geographically distributed data centers with failover
analysis_records.reasoning: High availability requires eliminating single points of failure. Redundant servers provide failover during hardware/software issues. Geographic distribution protects against site-level disasters. However, without confirmed architectural details, the effectiveness is uncertain.

risks.description: Architectural redundancy strategy is unspecified. Single points of failure may exist.
risks.rationale: The current knowledge state lists architectural approaches as 'Unknown'. Without designed redundancy (e.g., active-active clusters, automated failover), the 24/7 availability goal is at high risk.

non_risks.description: The business requirement for 24/7 operation is clearly defined and prioritized.
non_risks.rationale: The scenario is explicitly captured in the utility tree with high importance, providing a clear driver for architectural design.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Mean Time To Repair (MTTR) for failed components

tradeoff_points.parameter: Level of redundancy (number of redundant components)

scenario_reference.text: Credit-card terminal is supposed to request transaction processing at any time including peak-time and system should proceed all internal processing within one second besides external transaction processing with credit-card company.

analysis_records.stimulus: Transaction request from credit-card terminal
analysis_records.response_measure: Internal processing latency < 1 second
architectural_decisions: Use of asynchronous, non-blocking processing pipelines
Implementation of in-memory caches for frequent data (e.g., merchant info)
analysis_records.reasoning: To meet the 1-second internal processing goal under peak load, the system must avoid blocking operations and minimize database latency. Asynchronous processing decouples steps. Caching reduces data access times. Performance is highly sensitive to peak load volume and external service latency, which are unknown parameters.

risks.description: Peak transaction load and external service (credit-card company) latency are unspecified. Internal 1s target may be unachievable if external calls are slow or load exceeds capacity.
risks.rationale: Missing quantitative parameters (requests/sec, network latency) prevent accurate capacity planning. The architecture's ability to handle peak load is unverified.

non_risks.description: The performance goal is explicitly scoped to 'internal processing', isolating it from external network variability.
non_risks.rationale: This clear scope allows architects to focus optimization efforts on the system's internal components.

conflicting_attributes: Consistency (negative effect if stale data is served)

scenario_reference.text: System should ensure the information integrity with credit-card company.

analysis_records.stimulus: Data transmission to/from external credit-card company
analysis_records.response_measure: Data integrity maintained (no undetected corruption or alteration)
architectural_decisions: Use of cryptographic hashes (e.g., HMAC) or digital signatures on messages
Use of secure, reliable transport protocols (e.g., TLS)
analysis_records.reasoning: Data integrity requires mechanisms to detect tampering or corruption during transmission and storage. Cryptographic integrity checks are standard. However, the specific implementation (algorithms, key management) and validation of the external party's adherence are unknown.

risks.description: Lack of specified integrity mechanism and shared protocols with the external credit-card company.
risks.rationale: Architectural approaches are 'Unknown'. Without a defined, mutually agreed-upon integrity protocol (e.g., specific hashing algorithm, key exchange), data corruption or man-in-the-middle attacks may go undetected.

non_risks.description: Integrity is identified as a high-priority business requirement.
non_risks.rationale: Its high importance in the utility tree ensures it should receive adequate design attention.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Strength of cryptographic hash algorithm (e.g., SHA-256 vs. SHA-512)

conflicting_attributes: Performance (negative effect due to computation time)

scenario_reference.text: System should be synchronized in real-time with backup system and database of NIBS.

analysis_records.stimulus: Data write or update in the primary system
analysis_records.response_measure: Real-time synchronization (minimal replication lag)
architectural_decisions: Use of synchronous replication or a distributed consensus protocol (e.g., Raft)
Implementation of a change data capture (CDC) pipeline
analysis_records.reasoning: Real-time synchronization requires immediate propagation of changes. Synchronous replication ensures consistency but impacts write latency. The choice depends on the tolerance for lag vs. performance impact. The 'NIBS' backup system's capabilities and network characteristics are unknown.

risks.description: Synchronization mechanism and network performance to the NIBS backup are unspecified. 'Real-time' is ambiguous without a measurable lag threshold.
risks.rationale: Without defined architecture (e.g., synchronous vs. asynchronous replication) and network parameters (bandwidth, latency), the system may not achieve the required synchronization, risking data loss during failover.

non_risks.description: The requirement explicitly identifies a backup target (NIBS), providing a clear synchronization endpoint.
non_risks.rationale: This specificity reduces ambiguity compared to a generic backup requirement.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Network latency and bandwidth between primary and backup sites

conflicting_attributes: Performance/Writability (negative effect for synchronous due to increased latency)

addressed_attributes.rationale: Hard-coded message transformations optimize processing speed to meet the strict 1-second internal processing deadline for transaction handling

architectural_approaches.description: Continuous synchronization mechanism with backup system and NIBS database to ensure data consistency and immediate failover capability

addressed_attributes.rationale: Ensures data integrity and system continuity through redundant synchronized systems, preventing data loss during failures
Enables seamless failover and recovery operations without manual intervention or service disruption

architectural_approaches.description: Fault-tolerant hardware interface architecture for receiving and processing credit card terminal transactions with built-in redundancy

addressed_attributes.rationale: TANDEM systems are specifically designed for continuous operation and high availability through hardware-level fault tolerance
Provides secure transaction reception from terminals with built-in protection mechanisms for financial data

scenarios.scenario_text: Source: Credit card terminal. Stimulus: Transaction processing request arrives during normal operations. Artifact: Transaction processing subsystem with hard-coded message transformations. Environment: System operating under normal load conditions. Response: System completes all internal processing (message transformation, validation, routing). Response Measure: Internal processing completes within 1 second, excluding external credit-card company communication time.

Source: Multiple credit card terminals. Stimulus: High volume of concurrent transaction requests during peak business hours. Artifact: TANDEM receiving interface and transaction processing pipeline. Environment: Peak load conditions with maximum expected transaction volume. Response: System processes all transactions without queuing delays or performance degradation. Response Measure: Transaction throughput maintains baseline performance levels with <1 second internal processing time per transaction.

Source: Business operations requirement. Stimulus: Continuous operation demand over 24-hour period across all calendar days. Artifact: Entire credit card transaction system including TANDEM interface. Environment: Production environment with no planned maintenance windows. Response: System remains operational and accepts transaction requests. Response Measure: System uptime of 99.9%+ with 24/7/365 availability, zero planned downtime.

Source: Primary system component. Stimulus: Hardware or software failure occurs in primary transaction processing system. Artifact: Primary system, backup system, and real-time synchronization mechanism. Environment: Active transaction processing during failure event. Response: Backup system assumes processing responsibilities without service interruption. Response Measure: Failover completes with zero transaction loss and service interruption <5 seconds.

Source: Primary transaction processing system. Stimulus: Transaction data updates occur continuously during normal operations. Artifact: Real-time synchronization pattern between primary and backup systems. Environment: Normal operational state with active transaction processing. Response: Backup system receives and applies all data changes in real-time. Response Measure: Synchronization lag <100 milliseconds, zero data loss during synchronization.

Source: Transaction processing system. Stimulus: Transaction records and state changes generated during processing. Artifact: NIBS database synchronization interface and mechanism. Environment: Continuous operation with ongoing transactions. Response: NIBS database reflects current system state accurately. Response Measure: Database synchronization maintains consistency with <500 millisecond lag, zero data inconsistencies.

Source: Credit card company interface. Stimulus: Bidirectional transaction data exchange during authorization and settlement. Artifact: Message transformation layer and credit-card company communication interface. Environment: Production environment with active financial transactions. Response: System ensures data accuracy and prevents corruption during transmission. Response Measure: 100% data integrity verification, zero transaction data corruption or loss, cryptographic validation of all exchanges.

Source: Credit card terminal. Stimulus: Terminal initiates transaction request with sensitive cardholder data. Artifact: TANDEM receiving interface with built-in security mechanisms. Environment: Public-facing terminal network with potential security threats. Response: System receives and processes terminal data securely with encryption and authentication. Response Measure: All terminal communications encrypted, authentication successful for 100% of legitimate requests, zero unauthorized access incidents.

Source: System monitoring component. Stimulus: Primary system failure detected requiring failover. Artifact: Automated failover mechanism and real-time synchronization pattern. Environment: Production environment with active transactions and no operator intervention available. Response: System automatically initiates failover to backup without manual intervention. Response Measure: Failover completes automatically within 5 seconds, zero manual steps required, operators notified post-failover.

Source: System operator. Stimulus: Operator needs to assess system health and transaction processing status. Artifact: System monitoring and management interface. Environment: Normal operations with operator workstation access. Response: System provides real-time visibility into performance metrics, transaction volumes, and system health. Response Measure: Monitoring dashboard updates within 2 seconds, displays key metrics (transaction rate, processing time, system status, error rates).

Source: Terminal operator (cashier/merchant). Stimulus: Operator initiates transaction through credit card terminal interface. Artifact: Terminal user interface and transaction processing feedback mechanism. Environment: Point-of-sale environment during customer checkout. Response: Terminal provides immediate feedback and responsive interaction. Response Measure: Terminal acknowledges input within 200 milliseconds, displays transaction status updates in real-time, provides clear success/failure indication.

analysis_records.environment: Normal load conditions with active transaction processing
analysis_records.stimulus: Transaction processing request from credit card terminal
analysis_records.response_measure: Internal processing time < 1 second
architectural_decisions: Hard-coded message transformations for optimized processing speed
Financial System Architectural Style Pool with domain-specific patterns
TANDEM receiving interface for fault-tolerant transaction reception
analysis_records.reasoning: Hard-coded transformations eliminate runtime interpretation overhead, directly supporting the 1-second processing deadline. The domain-specific architectural style pool provides pre-optimized patterns for financial transactions. However, the tight coupling between transformation logic and system components creates maintainability challenges and potential performance bottlenecks if message formats change.

risks.description: Hard-coded message transformations may become performance bottleneck if message formats evolve or increase in complexity
risks.rationale: Any change to message structure requires code modification, recompilation, and redeployment, potentially causing service disruption and failing to meet the 1-second deadline during transition periods

risks.description: Processing pipeline may not scale efficiently under unexpected load spikes beyond normal conditions
risks.rationale: The architecture is optimized for normal load; sudden spikes could saturate the hard-coded transformation pipeline, causing queue buildup and deadline violations

non_risks.description: Hard-coded transformations adequately support the 1-second deadline under normal load
non_risks.rationale: Domain-specific optimization and elimination of runtime interpretation overhead provide sufficient performance margin for the specified response measure

sensitivity_points.parameter: Message transformation complexity (number of fields, validation rules)
CPU allocation to transformation processing threads

Critical dependency on accurate capacity planning and load distribution mechanisms to prevent bottlenecks during peak periods.

risks.rationale: Synchronization overhead competes for CPU, memory, and I/O resources during high transaction volumes, potentially degrading transaction processing performance

non_risks.rationale: TANDEM systems are specifically designed for high-volume transaction processing with built-in parallelism and load distribution

analysis_records.environment: Production environment with continuous operation requirement

architectural_decisions: TANDEM fault-tolerant hardware architecture for continuous operation
Real-time synchronization with backup system for failover capability
Redundant component design eliminating single points of failure
analysis_records.reasoning: TANDEM architecture provides hardware-level fault tolerance supporting continuous operation. Real-time backup synchronization enables immediate failover without service interruption. The 99.9% uptime target allows approximately 8.76 hours of downtime per year, which must accommodate only unplanned failures since planned downtime is prohibited.

risks.description: Software updates and patches cannot be applied without violating zero planned downtime requirement
risks.rationale: Without hot-swap or rolling update capability, critical security patches and bug fixes may require service interruption, creating a conflict between availability and security/reliability

risks.description: Cascading failure between primary and backup systems could violate availability target
risks.rationale: If a common-mode failure (e.g., software bug, network partition) affects both primary and backup simultaneously, the system loses redundancy and may experience extended downtime

non_risks.description: TANDEM hardware architecture adequately supports 99.9%+ availability requirement
non_risks.rationale: TANDEM systems are proven for high-availability applications with built-in redundancy at hardware level, well-suited for the 99.9% uptime target

sensitivity_points.parameter: Mean Time Between Failures (MTBF) of TANDEM hardware components
Mean Time To Repair (MTTR) for component failures

conflicting_attributes: Availability (positive: zero downtime requires hot-swap capability)
