analysis_records.environment: Active transaction processing during failure event
analysis_records.stimulus: Hardware or software failure in primary system
analysis_records.response_measure: Failover <5 seconds with zero transaction loss
architectural_decisions: Real-time synchronization pattern maintaining backup system currency
Automated failover mechanism for rapid transition
TANDEM interface redundancy for continuous transaction reception
analysis_records.reasoning: Real-time synchronization ensures backup system maintains current state, enabling rapid failover. The 5-second failover window requires automated detection and transition mechanisms. Zero transaction loss depends on synchronization lag being minimal and in-flight transaction handling during failover.

risks.description: In-flight transactions during failover may be lost if not properly handled by synchronization mechanism
risks.rationale: Transactions being processed at the moment of failure may not be fully synchronized to backup, violating the zero transaction loss requirement unless explicit transaction journaling and replay mechanisms exist

risks.description: Failover detection time may exceed budget if failure is subtle or gradual
risks.rationale: The 5-second failover window includes detection time; slow-developing failures (e.g., performance degradation, partial failures) may not trigger failover quickly enough

risks.description: Network partition between primary and backup could cause split-brain scenario
risks.rationale: If synchronization link fails but both systems remain operational, both may attempt to process transactions independently, causing data inconsistency and potential transaction duplication

non_risks.description: Real-time synchronization adequately supports zero transaction loss for committed transactions
non_risks.rationale: Synchronization pattern ensures backup system has current state for all completed transactions, enabling seamless continuation after failover

sensitivity_points.parameter: Synchronization lag between primary and backup
Failure detection threshold and timeout values

conflicting_attributes: Availability (positive: aggressive detection enables faster failover)
Stability (negative: aggressive detection may cause false-positive failovers)

analysis_records.environment: Normal operational state with active transaction processing
analysis_records.stimulus: Continuous transaction data updates
analysis_records.response_measure: Synchronization lag <100ms with zero data loss
architectural_decisions: Real-time synchronization pattern with continuous data replication
Dedicated synchronization channel between primary and backup
Transaction-level consistency guarantees
analysis_records.reasoning: The 100ms synchronization lag requirement ensures backup system remains current enough to support the 5-second failover target with minimal data loss. Synchronization must handle peak transaction volumes without falling behind. Network bandwidth and processing overhead are critical constraints.

risks.description: Synchronization lag may exceed 100ms during peak transaction volumes
risks.rationale: High transaction rates generate large volumes of synchronization data; if network bandwidth or backup system processing capacity is insufficient, synchronization will fall behind the 100ms target

risks.description: Synchronization mechanism failure creates single point of failure for data consistency

non_risks.description: Real-time synchronization pattern adequately supports 100ms lag target under normal load

analysis_records.stimulus: Transaction records and state changes
analysis_records.response_measure: Database sync <500ms lag with zero inconsistencies
architectural_decisions: NIBS database synchronization interface for external data consistency
Asynchronous synchronization mechanism to avoid blocking transaction processing
Consistency verification and reconciliation procedures
analysis_records.reasoning: The 500ms synchronization lag for NIBS database is more relaxed than the 100ms backup synchronization, suggesting NIBS serves reporting or secondary functions rather than failover. Asynchronous synchronization prevents database writes from blocking transaction processing, but introduces consistency challenges.

risks.description: Asynchronous NIBS synchronization may create temporary inconsistencies visible to external systems
risks.rationale: The 500ms lag window means NIBS database may show stale data; if external systems query NIBS during this window, they receive inconsistent information that could affect business decisions

risks.description: Database synchronization failures may go undetected, causing persistent inconsistencies
risks.rationale: Without robust verification and reconciliation mechanisms, failed synchronization operations could leave NIBS database permanently out of sync with transaction system state

non_risks.description: 500ms synchronization lag is acceptable for NIBS database use cases
non_risks.rationale: The relaxed lag requirement compared to backup synchronization suggests NIBS serves non-critical functions where eventual consistency is sufficient

conflicting_attributes: Reliability (positive: frequent sync reduces inconsistency window)
Performance (negative: frequent sync increases database load and network overhead)

Cryptographic validation for all credit-card company exchanges
End-to-end data integrity checks
analysis_records.reasoning: Financial transaction data requires absolute integrity; any corruption or loss could result in financial discrepancies, regulatory violations, or fraud. Cryptographic validation ensures authenticity and integrity. Hard-coded transformations must maintain data fidelity during format conversions.

risks.description: Hard-coded message transformations may introduce data corruption bugs during format conversions
risks.rationale: Complex transformation logic, especially when hard-coded, is prone to edge cases and bugs that could corrupt data fields, violating the 100% integrity requirement

risks.description: Cryptographic key management failures could compromise validation integrity
risks.rationale: If cryptographic keys are compromised, rotated improperly, or become desynchronized with credit card company, validation may fail or accept invalid data

non_risks.description: Cryptographic validation adequately ensures data integrity for credit-card company exchanges
non_risks.rationale: Industry-standard cryptographic mechanisms provide strong guarantees against data corruption and tampering during transmission

risks.description: Encryption implementation weaknesses could expose cardholder data during transmission

scenario_reference.text: Source: System monitoring component. Stimulus: Primary system failure detected requiring failover. Artifact: Automated failover mechanism and real-time synchronization pattern. Environment: Production environment with active transactions and no operator intervention available. Response: System automatically initiates failover to backup without manual intervention. Response Measure: Failover completes automatically within 5 seconds, zero manual steps required, operators notified post-failover.

analysis_records.environment: Production with no operator intervention available
analysis_records.stimulus: Primary system failure detection
analysis_records.response_measure: Automatic failover <5 seconds, zero manual steps, post-failover notification
architectural_decisions: Automated failover mechanism with no manual intervention requirement
Real-time synchronization enabling immediate backup activation
Post-failover operator notification system
analysis_records.reasoning: Automated failover eliminates human reaction time and potential errors, supporting the 5-second failover window. Operator notification after failover allows for investigation and remediation without blocking the failover process. Requires robust failure detection and decision-making logic.

risks.description: Automated failover may trigger incorrectly on transient issues, causing unnecessary service disruption
risks.rationale: Overly sensitive failure detection could cause false-positive failovers during temporary network glitches or performance spikes, creating instability and potential data inconsistency

risks.description: Operator notification failures could delay problem diagnosis and recovery
risks.rationale: If post-failover notifications fail to reach operators, they may remain unaware of the failure, delaying investigation and potential return to primary system

non_risks.description: Automated failover adequately supports 5-second failover requirement without manual intervention
non_risks.rationale: Automation eliminates human reaction time, enabling rapid failover that would be impossible with manual processes

sensitivity_points.parameter: Failure detection threshold and confidence level

conflicting_attributes: Operability (positive: full automation enables rapid failover)
Safety (negative: automation may trigger incorrectly without human judgment)

evaluation_inputs.system_description: Wargame 2000 is a real-time, human-in-the-loop ballistic missile defense simulation system. It is designed to model concepts of operation, doctrine, and tactics in a realistic combat environment. The system supports distributed discrete event simulation, allowing for the integration of dissimilar parts and interoperability with other simulations via High Level Architecture (HLA).

phase_1_discovery.initial_documentation_status: Documentation existed in Rational Rose/UML but was considered weak for capturing discrete events. Some architectural drawings caused stakeholder confusion and required real-time refinement.
evaluator_inquiry_questions: How are discrete simulation events represented in the static UML models?
Can you clarify the data flow in this architectural diagram to resolve stakeholder confusion?
How does the code reuse strategy align with the need for high-fidelity discrete event simulation?

hardware_view_description: Distributed simulation environment capable of hosting online, offsite, and multiple simultaneous games.
Networked command centers allowing participants to play from their own locations.
runtime_constraints: Must support 'Firm' real-time deadlines (statistical adherence).
Must provide 'Margin' (running faster than real-time) to support future requirements.

questions: How does the client-server separation impact the latency requirements for the human-in-the-loop displays?
How does the publish/subscribe mechanism handle peak load during high-density missile scenarios?

analysis_records.stimulus: Simulation controller initiates execution
analysis_records.response_measure: All processes start and run within required real-time deadlines (deadline unspecified).
architectural_decisions: Distributed Discrete Event Simulation architecture
Client-Server / Distributed topology
analysis_records.reasoning: The distributed architecture supports parallel process initiation, which can reduce startup latency. However, network latency and synchronization overhead between nodes could impact the ability to meet firm real-time deadlines, especially if deadlines are stringent (e.g., <100ms). The HLA runtime may introduce additional latency for time management.

risks.description: Network latency or synchronization delays may cause the simulation startup to miss real-time deadlines, affecting human-in-the-loop displays.
risks.rationale: Distributed coordination requires message passing; without guaranteed low-latency network, deadlines may be violated.

non_risks.description: Distributed architecture inherently supports parallel process startup, reducing sequential bottlenecks.
non_risks.rationale: Multiple processes can be launched concurrently across nodes, improving startup performance.

sensitivity_points.parameter: HLA Runtime Infrastructure (RTI) time management overhead

analysis_records.response_measure: Change implemented and tested within one game cycle (cycle duration unspecified).

Use of configuration files or rule engines
analysis_records.reasoning: If the rule set is encapsulated in a modular component with well-defined interfaces, changes can be isolated. However, if rules are hard-coded or tightly coupled with other simulation logic, modification may require extensive regression testing, risking missing the deadline.

risks.description: Tight coupling between rule logic and other simulation components may increase change effort, causing delays.
risks.rationale: Poor modularity can lead to widespread code changes and testing overhead.

non_risks.description: Use of a dedicated rule engine or configuration file allows quick updates without code recompilation.
non_risks.rationale: Separation of rules from core logic supports rapid modification.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Coupling between rule set and target assigner core logic

risks.description: New weapon system may require changes to HLA federation agreements or object models, delaying release.
risks.rationale: Interoperability standards impose coordination overhead with other simulations.

non_risks.description: Plugin architecture isolates new weapon code, minimizing impact on existing systems.
non_risks.rationale: Well-defined interfaces allow incremental addition.

scenario_reference.text: During normal operations, human-in-the-loop displays must maintain max instantaneous lag < 5 seconds and max average lag < 3 seconds to support operator decision-making.

analysis_records.environment: Normal operations with distributed human-in-the-loop displays across networked command centers
analysis_records.stimulus: Continuous stream of simulation events requiring real-time display updates
analysis_records.response_measure: Max instantaneous lag < 5 seconds, max average lag < 3 seconds
architectural_decisions: Client-Server separation with distributed architecture
Publish/Subscribe mechanism for event distribution
Network bandwidth allocation for display updates
analysis_records.reasoning: The client-server architecture enables distributed displays but introduces network latency. The publish/subscribe mechanism must efficiently route display-relevant events to minimize propagation delays. Meeting the 3-second average and 5-second instantaneous lag constraints requires careful network provisioning and event filtering to prevent display clients from being overwhelmed.

risks.description: Network latency variability in distributed environment may cause instantaneous lag to exceed 5-second threshold
risks.rationale: Wide-area network connections to offsite command centers are subject to congestion and routing variability beyond system control, potentially violating hard real-time constraints for human operators

risks.description: Publish/Subscribe event flooding during peak scenarios may overwhelm display clients
risks.rationale: High-density missile scenarios generate massive event volumes; without proper filtering and prioritization, display clients may experience processing backlogs leading to lag accumulation

non_risks.description: Average lag constraint of 3 seconds provides sufficient margin for typical network conditions
non_risks.rationale: The 3-second average allows for occasional spikes while maintaining acceptable operator experience under normal network conditions with proper event prioritization

sensitivity_points.parameter: Network bandwidth between server and distributed clients
Event filtering granularity in publish/subscribe mechanism

scenario_reference.text: Simulation controller initiates simulation execution, starts subordinate processes, and completes initialization from T=-infinity to T=0 within 10 minutes.

analysis_records.environment: System startup with distributed simulation components across multiple nodes
analysis_records.stimulus: Simulation controller initiates execution sequence
analysis_records.response_measure: Complete initialization within 10 minutes
architectural_decisions: Distributed discrete event simulation with coordinated initialization
Client-server architecture requiring process orchestration
HLA compliance with federation initialization protocols
analysis_records.reasoning: The 10-minute initialization window must accommodate starting distributed processes, establishing network connections, synchronizing initial state across all nodes, and completing HLA federation join procedures. The distributed architecture adds complexity compared to monolithic systems but provides necessary scalability.

risks.description: Distributed process startup dependencies may create initialization bottlenecks
risks.rationale: Sequential dependencies in initialization (e.g., server must start before clients) combined with network delays could approach or exceed the 10-minute budget if not carefully orchestrated

non_risks.description: 10-minute window provides adequate margin for typical initialization sequences
non_risks.rationale: Modern distributed systems can typically complete process startup and state synchronization within minutes; the 10-minute budget allows for reasonable fault recovery

sensitivity_points.parameter: Initial state data volume requiring synchronization

scenario_reference.text: System runs faster than real-time to provide margin for future requirements and support monthly exercise turnaround frequency.

analysis_records.environment: Normal simulation execution without human-in-the-loop constraints
analysis_records.stimulus: Simulation execution of combat scenarios
analysis_records.response_measure: Execution speed > 1x real-time
architectural_decisions: Distributed discrete event simulation with optimized event processing
Publish/Subscribe mechanism for efficient event routing
Separation of human-in-the-loop displays from core simulation
analysis_records.reasoning: Faster-than-real-time execution requires efficient event processing and minimal synchronization overhead. The distributed architecture must balance parallelism benefits against coordination costs. Decoupling displays allows core simulation to run at maximum speed when human interaction is not required.

risks.description: Distributed synchronization overhead may prevent faster-than-real-time execution
risks.rationale: Discrete event simulation across distributed nodes requires frequent synchronization to maintain causality; this overhead could limit speedup, especially during high-density scenarios with many inter-node dependencies

non_risks.description: Publish/Subscribe decoupling enables core simulation to run independently of display constraints
non_risks.rationale: When displays are not active, the simulation can execute at maximum speed without being throttled by human-in-the-loop lag requirements

sensitivity_points.parameter: Event processing capacity per simulation node

scenario_reference.text: During high-density missile scenario peak load, publish/subscribe mechanism maintains real-time deadlines without degradation.

analysis_records.environment: Peak load conditions with high-density missile scenario generating maximum event volume
analysis_records.stimulus: Massive simultaneous missile launches creating event storm
analysis_records.response_measure: Maintain real-time deadlines without degradation
architectural_decisions: Publish/Subscribe mechanism with scalable event routing
Event prioritization and filtering strategies
Distributed processing to handle peak loads
analysis_records.reasoning: High-density missile scenarios represent worst-case load conditions. The publish/subscribe mechanism must scale to handle event storms while maintaining real-time responsiveness. This requires efficient routing algorithms, adequate network bandwidth, and possibly event aggregation or filtering to prevent subscriber overload.

risks.description: Publish/Subscribe broker may become bottleneck during peak event storms
risks.rationale: Centralized or insufficiently distributed pub/sub infrastructure could saturate under high-density missile scenario loads, causing event queuing delays that violate real-time deadlines

risks.description: Network bandwidth saturation during peak loads may cause event delivery delays
risks.rationale: High-density scenarios generate correlated event bursts that could exceed network capacity, particularly on links to distributed command centers

non_risks.description: Event filtering and prioritization can reduce load on non-critical subscribers
non_risks.rationale: Publish/Subscribe pattern allows selective event delivery; subscribers can filter irrelevant events, reducing processing load during peak scenarios

scenario_reference.text: Change joint firing doctrine rule set in the automated weapon target assigner in time for the next game (within 1 month exercise cycle).

analysis_records.environment: Development and testing environment between exercises
analysis_records.stimulus: Request to modify firing doctrine rules
analysis_records.response_measure: Complete modification within 1 month exercise cycle
architectural_decisions: Modular rule-based architecture for doctrine representation
Separation of doctrine rules from core simulation logic
Testing framework for validating rule changes
analysis_records.reasoning: Meeting the 1-month cycle requires doctrine rules to be externalized from core code, ideally in declarative format. The publish/subscribe mechanism supports loose coupling between doctrine components and simulation. Testing must be efficient to validate changes within the time budget.

risks.description: Doctrine rule changes may have unforeseen interactions with other simulation components
risks.rationale: Complex rule sets can have non-obvious dependencies; insufficient testing time within the 1-month cycle could allow defects to reach production exercises

non_risks.description: 1-month cycle provides adequate time for isolated rule set modifications
non_risks.rationale: If doctrine rules are properly modularized and externalized, simple rule changes can be implemented and tested within weeks

sensitivity_points.parameter: Degree of coupling between doctrine rules and core simulation

Publish/Subscribe mechanism for loose coupling
Distributed discrete event simulation supporting heterogeneous entities

The publish/subscribe mechanism allows new components to subscribe to relevant events without modifying existing publishers. The discrete event simulation framework must accommodate new event types.

risks.rationale: New weapon systems often interact with detection, tracking, engagement, and damage assessment components; ripple effects could extend development time beyond release cycle

risks.description: Performance impact of cruise missile simulation may not be predictable until integration
risks.rationale: Cruise missiles have different flight profiles and engagement timelines than ballistic missiles; computational load and event generation patterns may stress the system differently

non_risks.description: HLA compliance facilitates integration of new entity types
non_risks.rationale: Standardized HLA interfaces and object models provide clear integration points for new simulation components

scenario_reference.text: Reconfigure Wargame 2000 from running a theater ballistic missile defense simulation to a national missile defense simulation in one week.

analysis_records.stimulus: Request to change mission scope from theater to national defense
analysis_records.response_measure: Complete reconfiguration within one week
architectural_decisions: Parameterized scenario configuration
Modular component architecture allowing substitution
Separation of scenario data from simulation logic
analysis_records.reasoning: The 1-week reconfiguration requirement is extremely aggressive for such a major scope change. This demands that theater vs. national differences be primarily configuration-driven rather than code-driven. Geographic scope, sensor coverage, weapon inventories, and threat characteristics must be parameterizable.

risks.description: One week is insufficient for major architectural changes required by theater-to-national transition
risks.rationale: Theater and national missile defense have fundamentally different scales, timelines, and engagement geometries; if these differences require code changes rather than configuration, 1 week is unrealistic

risks.description: Testing and validation cannot be thorough within 1-week timeframe
risks.rationale: Major reconfigurations introduce risk of subtle errors; 1 week allows minimal testing, potentially compromising exercise validity

sensitivity_points.parameter: Degree of parameterization vs. hard-coding of mission scope

scenario_reference.text: Integrate with other HLA-compliant simulations to serve as rapid prototyping facility for interoperability studies.

analysis_records.stimulus: Request to integrate with external HLA simulation
analysis_records.response_measure: Successful federation establishment and data exchange
architectural_decisions: HLA compliance with standardized FOM/SOM
Publish/Subscribe mechanism mapping to HLA RTI
Standardized object and interaction models
analysis_records.reasoning: HLA compliance is the primary architectural decision enabling this scenario. The system's internal publish/subscribe mechanism must map cleanly to HLA's RTI services. Standardized Federation Object Model (FOM) and Simulation Object Model (SOM) definitions are critical for semantic interoperability.

risks.description: Semantic mismatches between FOMs may require custom translation logic
risks.rationale: While HLA provides syntactic interoperability, different simulations may model entities and interactions differently, requiring mapping logic that undermines rapid prototyping goals

non_risks.description: HLA RTI handles low-level communication and synchronization
non_risks.rationale: HLA infrastructure provides proven mechanisms for distributed simulation coordination, reducing integration effort

sensitivity_points.parameter: Degree of FOM/SOM standardization across federates

analysis_records.environment: Distributed gaming environment with multiple concurrent exercises
analysis_records.stimulus: Multiple simultaneous exercises with geographically distributed participants
analysis_records.response_measure: Successful multi-game operation with participant connectivity
architectural_decisions: Client-Server architecture with distributed clients
Network infrastructure supporting multiple concurrent sessions
Session isolation and resource partitioning
analysis_records.reasoning: Supporting multiple simultaneous games requires session isolation to prevent cross-contamination while sharing infrastructure. The client-server architecture must scale to support multiple server instances or multi-tenant operation. Network design must accommodate concurrent games without interference.

risks.description: Resource contention between simultaneous games may cause performance degradation

scenario_reference.text: System maintains statistical adherence to firm real-time deadlines during continuous operation, with data collection window of 30 seconds post-termination.

analysis_records.response_measure: Statistical adherence to real-time deadlines (measured over 30-second windows)
architectural_decisions: Distributed discrete event simulation with deadline scheduling
Real-time operating system or priority scheduling
Monitoring and measurement infrastructure
analysis_records.reasoning: Firm real-time deadlines require predictable execution with bounded latency. The distributed architecture complicates this by introducing network delays and synchronization points. Statistical adherence (rather than absolute guarantees) suggests the system can tolerate occasional deadline misses but must maintain overall performance.

risks.description: Distributed synchronization may cause unpredictable deadline violations
risks.rationale: Network delays and remote node failures can cause cascading deadline misses that exceed acceptable statistical thresholds

non_risks.description: Statistical adherence allows for occasional transient overloads
non_risks.rationale: The 30-second measurement window permits short-term deadline misses as long as overall performance meets requirements

scenario_reference.text: Distributed discrete event simulation maintains timeline fidelity within 10% of EADSIM events to accurately answer the 'Big Five Questions' regarding operator knowledge and action timing.

analysis_records.environment: Combat scenario simulation requiring high-fidelity event timing
analysis_records.stimulus: Complex engagement scenarios with precise timing requirements
analysis_records.response_measure: Timeline accuracy within 10% of EADSIM reference
architectural_decisions: Distributed discrete event simulation with synchronized clocks
Event ordering and causality preservation mechanisms
High-resolution timing infrastructure
analysis_records.reasoning: The 10% fidelity requirement demands precise event timing across distributed nodes. Clock synchronization, event ordering, and causality preservation are critical. The distributed architecture introduces challenges because events on different nodes must maintain correct temporal relationships despite network delays.

risks.description: Clock drift between distributed nodes may accumulate beyond 10% tolerance
risks.rationale: Without robust clock synchronization (e.g., NTP, PTP), independent node clocks will drift, causing timeline divergence that violates fidelity requirements

risks.description: Network delays may cause event reordering that violates causality
risks.rationale: Events generated on different nodes may arrive out of order due to variable network delays, potentially causing incorrect simulation outcomes

non_risks.description: 10% tolerance provides reasonable margin for distributed timing variations
non_risks.rationale: The tolerance allows for small timing discrepancies inherent in distributed systems while maintaining sufficient accuracy for operator decision analysis

evaluation_inputs.system_description: WIN-T is the Army's tactical telecommunications system designed to provide a secure, high-speed, high-capacity, and high-mobility backbone communications network. It enables mobile communications using the Internet Protocol (IP) to provide integrated voice, data, and video. It connects the Global Information Grid (GIG) to the Future Force, extending from the Maneuver Battalion to the Theater Rear boundary.

phase_1_discovery.initial_documentation_status: The documentation was recently consolidated following the merger of two competing contractor teams. As a result, the initial architecture documentation contained inconsistencies, was excessively complex, and diagrams often had mixed heritage, leading to confusion and potential errors.
evaluator_inquiry_questions: How will the system handle the self-organization of nodes when requirements for the algorithms are not fully defined?
What are the specific interface definitions for the Service-Oriented Architecture given the reliance on emerging standards?
How does the architecture accommodate the transition from radio firmware to high-level network operations without explicit performance models?

hardware_view_description: The system must support mobile nodes (vehicles) communicating via Line-of-Sight radios and satellite links.
The topology includes tiered nodes ranging from Maneuver Battalions to Theater Rear boundaries, requiring 'on-the-move' connectivity.
runtime_constraints: Network bandwidth is severely limited during peak operational traffic, requiring strict QoS throttling.
The system must support 'on-the-move' throughput while traveling at speeds up to 25-45 mph.

questions: How does the Enterprise Application Integration Platform handle message latency across low-bandwidth satellite links?
How is loose coupling maintained between the NetOps management software and the radio transmission subsystems?

raw_candidate_scenarios.description: A collection of vehicles collects in a 'parking lot' during operations. The networks can self-organize and nodes configure themselves within 5 minutes.
A COTS product is becoming increasingly incompatible with other COTS products being used. The COTS product is replaced.
A unit is overrun during operations. The system detects the unauthorized users and generates a security alert; an authorized person can 'zeroize' the system and shut it down remotely.
A WIN-T gateway node has been corrupted due to a network intrusion. Intrusion and corruption is detected and another node takes over duties.

business_goals: Provide a single integrating communications network to function as the Army's tactical portion of the GIG
Link FCS with higher Army echelons and the GIG
Provide a reliable and secure network with high speed, high capacity, and high quality of service (QoS)
Support mobile communications and replace legacy systems (MSE, TRI-TAC, ISYSCON, Trojan Spirit)
Deploy a user-friendly human machine interface (HMI) for the WIN-T operator
Minimize the amount of network management the WIN-T operator must perform (automate planning)
Operable and maintainable within budget and schedule
Transparent to combat users and operators
technical_constraints: Long life cycle (fielding from 2008 through 2020, expected lifetime 20+ years)
Interoperable with Army Enterprise network, FCS, Joint networks, and Coalition network
Upgradeable (early spirals, block upgrades, COTS upgrades, security upgrades)

analysis_records.environment: Dynamic, mobile tactical network during force assembly.
analysis_records.stimulus: Multiple mobile nodes (vehicles) converge into a dense, ad-hoc network.
analysis_records.response_measure: Network self-organizes and nodes self-configure within 5 minutes.
architectural_decisions: Use of dynamic, self-organizing network protocols.
Implementation of a decoupled Message Bus for service communication.
analysis_records.reasoning: The Message Bus supports decoupled, asynchronous communication which is resilient to changing network topology. However, the 5-minute target is a strict performance requirement for the self-organizing protocols. The bus adds overhead; if protocol messages are large or frequent, latency during convergence could exceed the target.

risks.description: Self-organization protocols may not meet the 5-minute convergence target under high node density or poor RF conditions.
risks.rationale: The analysis lacks quantitative data on protocol performance, node count, and bandwidth, making this target unvalidated.

risks.description: The Message Bus could become a single point of failure or bottleneck during rapid network formation.
risks.rationale: If the bus instance is centralized or has limited throughput, the flood of discovery and configuration messages during convergence could degrade performance.

non_risks.description: The decoupled nature of the Message Bus inherently supports dynamic topology changes.
non_risks.rationale: Services communicate via the bus without direct dependencies, allowing nodes to join/leave without breaking point-to-point connections.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Message Bus throughput and latency during peak load

scenario_reference.text: A COTS product is becoming increasingly incompatible with other COTS products being used. The COTS product is replaced.

analysis_records.environment: Long-term system evolution over a 20+ year lifecycle.
analysis_records.stimulus: A COTS product requires replacement due to incompatibility.
analysis_records.response_measure: The product is replaced with minimal system disruption and reintegration effort.
architectural_decisions: Adoption of Service-Oriented Architecture (SOA) with standardized service contracts.
Encapsulation of COTS functionality within discrete, replaceable services.
analysis_records.reasoning: SOA promotes loose coupling and well-defined interfaces. If the COTS product is encapsulated behind a stable service contract, it can be swapped. Success depends on the contract's quality and the degree to which the COTS product's proprietary features are abstracted.

risks.description: Service contracts may be poorly designed or become outdated, creating tight coupling to the specific COTS product.
risks.rationale: If the contract mirrors the COTS API, replacing it requires changes to all service consumers, negating the benefit.

non_risks.description: The SOA style fundamentally supports component replacement.
non_risks.rationale: Modularity and standardized interfaces are core tenets of SOA, directly addressing this scenario.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Stability and completeness of service contracts

tradeoff_points.parameter: Level of abstraction in service contracts
conflicting_attributes: Performance (negative: potential for extra abstraction layers)

scenario_reference.text: A unit is overrun during operations. The system detects the unauthorized users and generates a security alert; an authorized person can 'zeroize' the system and shut it down remotely.

analysis_records.stimulus: Unauthorized physical access to a node.
analysis_records.response_measure: 1. Detect unauthorized access. 2. Generate alert. 3. Enable remote secure shutdown (zeroize).
architectural_decisions: Implementation of intrusion detection and alerting services.
Secure, authenticated remote command channel (likely via the Message Bus).
analysis_records.reasoning: Detection relies on monitoring services. The remote zeroize command must be authenticated, integrity-protected, and delivered reliably even if the node is partially compromised. The Message Bus can facilitate secure command dissemination but must itself be secured.

risks.description: Compromised node may ignore or block remote zeroize commands, or falsify detection alerts.
risks.rationale: If an attacker gains sufficient control, they can subvert the local security agent and communication stack.

risks.description: Lack of quantitative targets for detection time and command execution time.
risks.rationale: Without specific timing requirements, the effectiveness of the security response is undefined.

non_risks.description: A dedicated security service architecture aligns with the need for centralized monitoring and response.
non_risks.rationale: SOA allows for specialized security services to be developed and integrated.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Latency and reliability of the secure command channel under attack

scenario_reference.text: A WIN-T gateway node has been corrupted due to a network intrusion. Intrusion and corruption is detected and another node takes over duties.

analysis_records.stimulus: A critical gateway node is corrupted.
analysis_records.response_measure: 1. Detect intrusion and corruption. 2. Automatically failover duties to a healthy node.
architectural_decisions: Health monitoring and intrusion detection services.
Redundant node configuration and failover mechanisms.
Message Bus to facilitate rerouting of traffic.
analysis_records.reasoning: Detection is similar to RS-18. Failover requires: a) pre-designated or dynamically elected backup nodes, b) state replication or session recovery mechanisms for gateway duties, and c) rapid re-routing of network traffic. The Message Bus aids in disseminating failover commands and rerouting messages.

risks.description: Failover may cause service interruption or data loss if gateway state is not adequately replicated.
risks.rationale: Real-time state synchronization is complex and may impact performance. Lack of data on acceptable downtime.

risks.description: The corruption (e.g., malware) might propagate to backup nodes during state synchronization.
risks.rationale: Without clean-slate failover mechanisms, corrupted data or code could be transferred.

non_risks.description: The decoupled communication via the Message Bus simplifies rerouting traffic away from a failed node.
non_risks.rationale: Message endpoints are service-based, not node-based, allowing the bus to redirect to a new provider.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Frequency and granularity of node health state replication
Time to detect corruption and trigger failover

conflicting_attributes: Performance/Network Load (negative: consumes bandwidth and node resources)

system_context.system_description: A system offering voice, data and multimedia services over the company's Intranet, providing a global solution for communication in the enterprise environment.
system_context.business_goals: To provide a global solution for the communication in the enterprise environment; increase the offering of services for enterprise communications.

evaluation_setup.evaluation_goal: To evaluate two alternative software architectures with respect to extensibility, performance, and modifiability, addressing problems of the existing system.

architectures.name: H.323 Architecture
architectures.description: The existing architecture based on ITU-T H.323 protocol. It uses Terminal Agents to allow H.323 terminals to access the system and a SiteKeeper for routing and resource management.

key_components.responsibilities: Allows H.323 terminals to access the system; multiplexes message requests and responses.

Performs call control functions (Address Translation, Admission Control, Bandwidth Control).

architectures.name: SIP Architecture
architectures.description: A new architecture based on IETF SIP protocol. It introduces a Multiprotocol Access Controller (MAC) for protocol translation and uses SIP Proxies and Registrars.

key_components.responsibilities: Access point for terminals; provides protocol translation to HLTP and then to SIP (UAC/UAS level).
Performs terminal location, message sorting; Call Manager component manages SIP calls and user administration.
Manages the registration of SIP terminals.

architectural_strengths: SIP architecture performs better (fewer components and messages involved in basic call phases).

recommendations: Adoption of the SIP protocol architecture.
Use the proposed architecture as a pattern for systems with similar performance and extensibility requirements.

system_context.system_description: Architectures used for the generation of social head gaze in robots, mapping communicative and nonverbal functions to robot head gaze actions.
system_context.business_goals: To serve as a template for creating or re-engineering systems, provide analyses and understanding of different systems, and provide a common lexicon and taxonomy.

evaluation_setup.evaluation_goal: To evaluate, improve, and re-engineer existing head gaze system architectures, giving insight into their quality and determining if they meet requirements.

architectures.name: Human-Robot Collaboration Architecture
architectures.description: Supports engagement between a human and a humanoid robot by generating head gaze behaviors using specifications from human-human communication for conversational turn taking and engagement.

architectures.name: Robot Behavior Toolkit Architecture
architectures.description: Provides a framework for generating head gaze in human-like robots using specifications for conversational turn taking and referential gaze.

key_components.responsibilities: Collection of behavioral specifications in XML.
Queries the Knowledge Base for an appropriate behavior based on the percept.
Resolves conflicts and overlaps among behaviors by prioritization.
Provides internal and external percepts based on information from the Perceptual System and current action.

Coordination mechanisms exist in both Collaboration Manager and Maintenance Policy and are not fully isolated.
Serial flow of data between Turn Policy and Reference Policy affects real-time performance.

scenario_evaluations.change_description: Adaptation to different robots and dialog.
issues_identified: None significant; offers adequate support as subsystems are isolated and non-monolithic.

scenario_evaluations.change_description: Addition of new behaviors for multi-party scenario.
issues_identified: Collaboration Manager functionalities need upgrade and are monolithic.

scenario_evaluations.change_description: Incorporation of a new behavior.
issues_identified: Knowledge Base subsystem is monolithic.
Use of the same subsystem for different behaviors reduces maintainability and reusability.

architectural_strengths: RBT offers adequate support for re-engineering to new environments due to isolated, non-monolithic subsystems.
HRC components represent individual social head gaze functions well.
architectural_weaknesses: HRC has a monolithic Collaboration Manager with poor separation of concerns.
HRC has serial data flow between Turn and Reference policies.
RBT has a monolithic Knowledge Base.
RBT is limited to rule-based systems.
Both architectures lack nonverbal functions (Projecting Mental State, Establishing Agency).

architecture_comparison.rationale: Better support for adaptation to new environments due to isolated subsystems, though extension of capability is hindered by monolithic Knowledge Base.
Inadequate support for adaptation due to monolithic Collaboration Manager and serial dependencies affecting performance.

recommendations: For HRC: Isolate perception and coordination functions from the Collaboration Manager.
For HRC: Make Turn Policy independent of Reference Policy to improve real-time performance.
For RBT: Subdivide Knowledge Base into independent self-contained components.
For RBT: Upgrade subsystems to support advanced techniques like learning, not just rules.

system_context.system_description: A large non object oriented legacy system used by postal organizations that offer their customers specific services in order to manage big amounts of physical mail starting from electronic data files.
system_context.business_goals: Improve maintainability, reduce the time to close the change requests, and have a more agile IT system that can be adapted to change faster.

evaluation_setup.evaluation_goal: To compare two alternative architectures of the target postal system to understand whether a New Architecture based on SOA could reduce the maintenance/evolution times.

architectures.name: Actual Architecture
architectures.description: Reflects the real architecture of the current System. Electronic files are acquired by Front End, sent to Server, which creates SubServer processes. Batches are normalized, checked, cleaned, pre-generated, dispatched, generated and sent to Printing Centers.

key_components.responsibilities: Acquires electronic files (batches) submitted by customers and sends them to the Server.
Handles in parallel all received files; creates SubServer process for each batch.
Transforms batch inch by inch using Normalizer, Checker & Cleaner, and Pre-Generator & Generator.
Transforms data.
Checks and cleans data.
Generates output.
Stores relevant information; contains Dispatcher Stored Procedures.

assumptions: <If any>

architectures.name: New Architecture (SOA)
architectures.description: Based on SOA principles. The Server manages the parallel execution of several running orchestrators (the Batches) which call Web services.

key_components.responsibilities: Manages parallel execution of running orchestrators (Batches).
Calls Web services to fulfill tasks.
Realizes splitting of batches.
<Brief description>
<Brief description>

architectural_strengths: New Architecture requires fewer changes (modifications plus additions) to accommodate scenarios.

architectural_weaknesses: Actual Architecture requires more changes (35 vs 27).
Actual Architecture requires higher effort (11 High/21 Med vs 8 High/8 Med).
overall_results.modifiability_assessment: Preliminary results are in favour of the New Architecture that can be adapted to change faster than the actual one.

architecture_comparison.rationale: Requires fewer changes (27 vs 35) and less effort (more 'Low' effort changes, fewer 'High' effort changes) to fit the considered ten scenarios.
Requires more component modifications and additions, and higher estimated effort for the evaluated scenarios.

recommendations: Proceed with migration towards SOA (re-engineering) if the comparison is completely in favour of the New Architecture.
